speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR CONSIDERATION OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after discussions among the parties, a basic agreement has been reached as to the manner in which we should proceed, today, tomorrow and Friday with the business of supply.
As the House is aware, the main estimates have been discussed in the last parliament and in this parliament in standing committees, and there is a special order dealing with the remainder of the business and how to dispose of it by Friday afternoon. When orders of the day are called I understand there is agreement to dispose of the motion for concurrence in main estimates and of the motion for concurrence in supplementary estimates (A) without debate. The motion for first reading of the consequent appropriation bill is, of course, not debatable. I understand there is also agreement to dispose of the motion for second reading of the bill without debate. The House will then go into Committee of the Whole on the bill. I understand that there is agreement that all the clauses of the bill be stood and that the committee proceed directly to schedule A of the bill, which refers to the main estimates.
So that consideration of schedule A, that is, the main estimates, may be undertaken in an orderly fashion, it is my understanding that there is agreement that discussion should be organized in the following manner: First, for about an hour to an hour and one half, discussion would be on the estimates of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) and can, thereby, cover a broad range of matters relating to financial and personnel management of the government. Second, for about two and one half to three hours, discussion would be on the estimates of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). Third, for about two and one half to three hours, discussion would be on the estimates of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson). Fourth, for about two and one half to three hours, discussion would be on the estimates of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson). Fifth, for about two and one half to three hours, discussion would be on the estimates of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan). Sixth, for about two and one half to three hours, discussion would be on the estimates of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury).
I should explain that these departments were selected by the opposition parties as those on which they wished to concentrate their discussion. If there is still time remaining before the time on Friday when all outstanding questions must be put, discussion could cover other aspects of the bill, whether in committee of the whole or on third reading stage.
There is an understanding as well with respect to debate that, in order to give all members an opportunity of discussing these departments, each member should be restricted to one 20 minute speech in the committee on each department, but that this restriction would not apply in cases of direct questioning and answering. Nor would a minister be prevented from rebutting points made during the discussion.
It would be possible to make an order with regard to the plan that I have just outlined, but such an order might impose too much rigidity on the debate and I do not believe it will be necessary. If there is difficulty, the committee could rise, report progress and the House could then deal with the necessary order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR CONSIDERATION OF SUPPLY

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to inform hon. members we will now proceed to the study of the provisions of the schedule dealing with the Treasury Board which may be found at the bottom of page 28 and on page 29 of the bill.
On Schedule A-Treasury Board.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the appropriation bill before us relates to the main estimates and the first supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year.
As most hon. members will recall, I am sure, the main estimates were presented to the last Parliament on February 28 and shortly before the beginning of the current fiscal year Parliament voted interim supply to be used for the public service until the end of June.
In May, Parliament was dissolved and general elections were called. Since interim supply ran out at the beginning of summer, the government has financed itself through a series of special warrants, each covering approximately one month. Section 23 of the Financial Administration Act provides that such warrants can be issued to get the funds needed when Parliament is not sitting. The last of these warrants which was prepared in September should be barely enough to cover expenditures for October.
Almost all the expenditures incurred between the months of June and October were already in the main estimates, so that almost all the warrants were, so to speak, an advance on the estimates, the few new items are provided for in the supplementary estimates. In fact, except for two votes, the whole supplementary estimates include items that were covered by the special warrants, but not the main estimates.
The first of these two items deals with the payment of compensation on imports of oil and oil products (Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, vote 52a, $330 million) which will be handled by the Energy Supplies Allocation Board. It covers the months of November and December. Before then, I hope that Parliament will have adopted further legislation to provide for these payments until the end of the fiscal year.
The second deals with payments provided for in the program for the double price of wheat (Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, credit 41a, $79,300,000), in order to subsidize the price of wheat for Canadian consumers between the month of September 1973 and July 1974. The bill concerning the other six years of this 7-year program has reached the second reading stage in the House.
The appropriation bill we are discussing today would grant the total credits of the main estimates and the supplementary estimates for the rest of the fiscal year.
To give the usual assurances, Mr. Chairman, I must mention that this bill is along the same lines as those of years past and does not contain any new authority to borrow.

October 23, 1974
Estimates

I would like to summarize very briefly what the estimates contain. If we take main estimates of $22 billion, supplementary estimates of $890 million, and for completeness the forecast of payment for old age security and the guaranteed income supplement of $3.4 billion, we have, for total budgetary estimates to date, a figure of almost $26.3 billion.
To avoid any confusion I want to remind hon. members that the figure my colleague, the Minister of Finance, will use when talking about total government outlays at the time of the budget will differ from the figures I have available now. There is always a net lapse or shortfall of a few hundred million between estimates and actual expenditures reflecting such things as delays in filling vacant positions and delays in construction. In addition, the Minister of Finance will provide in his figures for a contingency to cover expenditure requirements that may yet arise.
In any case, to talk in broad terms, an amount of about $15 billion of the $26 billion presented to date in what are called budgetary expenditures is devoted to transfer payments. That is 57 per cent. The largest of these transfer payments are: old age security and the guaranteed income supplement; family allowance payments; unconditional fiscal transfers to the provinces; the conditional or special purpose transfers to the provinces to cover half the costs for hospital care, medical care, and the Canada Assistance Plan; veterans' pensions and allowances; the government's share of the cost of unemployment insurance payments; grants to the less developed countries; and the subsidies recently introduced to ease the impact at the consumer level of price pressure on milk, bread, and petroleum products.
Most of these, accounting for about $10 billion, are measures successive Liberal governments have taken to give Canada systems of social security worthy of a modern, relatively wealthy state.
Other redistribution measures designed to promote equality of treatment for our citizens, such as fiscal transfer payments to the provinces and support for university education, call for expenditures approaching another $3 billion. Almost all the foregoing are transfer payments governed by statute, and some are covered by five-year agreements with the provinces. Most of those who criticize government expenditures are very unhelpful as to what specifically might be done to reduce them. But even if we were to have a government so unenlightened as to wish to tear down these key supports of our national life, years might well elapse before the destruction would be carried out.
In practice then, the great bulk of the expenditures of the federal government must be taken as given. Only at the margin is there room to manoeuvre so as to tune the long term pattern of expenditures which has been put in place over a decade, and more so as to respond to new demands or to try to affect the movement of the economy.
The rest, about $11 billion or 43 per cent, covers the servicing of the public debt, about $3 billion; the subsidization of Crown corporations, about three quarters of a

billion dollars; and the remainder, the operating and capital costs of departments.
I might note that an important reason for the growth in the size of the public debt is the money borrowed to meet non budgetary requirements which take the form of investment in Crown corporations-CMHC, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the Farm Credit Corporation, the Export Development Corporation, and so on-Crown corporations being special instruments in the furthering of the social, economic and other policies.
About one third of the operating costs of the government for 1974-75 are taken up in the defence budget, and most of the rest in programs of service to the public, such as the Post Office and transport services, or in the essential functions of government as government, such as tax collection and the RCMP.
It is important to recognize, though it seems easy for some critics to forget, that the federal government provides and must pay for a wide range of basic services for the economy-airports, air traffic control, the mails, food and drug inspection, federal police-the list could go on a long time. These services become more vital and more expensive as society grows, and in all realism they should be looked upon as being only slightly more optional than the redistribution measures established by statute to which I previously referred.

So there, Mr. Chairman, you have in short an idea of the situation before the House at the present time. As the hon. members will realize, more than half the federal budget is provided under acts passed by the House and over which we have practically no control, unless of course the House wishes to introduce new bills. We are now trying to check the level of government expenditures as much as possible. Over the last three months, we have given instructions to all departments to the effect that they must operate within the limits of the estimates tabled in the House today.
A few supplementary expenditures now before the House are the result of measures carried by the government and requested by the House of Commons, such as the one-price oil policy and the one-price wheat policy for Canadian consumers. I hope hon. members will understand that if they want this governmet to be able to control the growth in government expenditures, they cannot at the same time ask us to make further expenditures.
Therefore, I urge hon. members in the next three days to meditate on this aspect of the issue. I will be glad to answer questions from hon. members. The other ministers referred to with respect to the order introduced in the House for the debate on the current estimates and the supplementary estimates will be present to answer questions which I hope will be useful to hon. members and Canadians in general so it will be realized that federal government activities are quite important. The larger part of government expenditures, 57 per cent, are set out in legislation voted by hon. members. It would probably be quite improper, for example, for the President of the Treasury Board to propose cuts in old age security pensions, family allowances or other programs of this type.
October 23, 1974

That is why we are here today, to explain the estimates and give the necessary information to hon. members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the minister on his able presentation of the estimates and wish him well in the very difficult task which lies ahead of him. I can only assume that he took it over because he was a refugee from his last job, and anything was a good escape hatch.
In my opinion this bill is wrongly called an appropriation bill. I suggest it could better be named the misappropriation bill because it is nothing but the legalization of the $25 billion rip-off of the Canadian taxpayer by the Trudeau government.
To take money from people with their consent and, after adequate opportunity, to examine the purpose and scrutinize the detail, are one thing, but the ritualistic tribal dance which we call approving estimates is merely a farce, a slapstick comedy. Any suggestion that the existing rules and regulations permit members of parliament to engage in a meaningful check on the gigantic spending program of the government is absolute nonsense.
Author?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The traditional right to withhold supply until all grievances have been dealt with and parliament is satisfied with the bona fide of proposed expenditures is gone. It has been swept away by an arrogant executive.
As we pass through the twilight of the bureaucratic dominated welfare state to the darkness that lies beyond, we find it quite impossible as members of parliament to carry out our rights and duties of ensuring that money, extracted as taxes from the people of Canada, is properly spent.
There are many reasons for this but time permits me to deal with just a few in a limited form. First there is the sheer size of the public accounts and of the blue book of estimates, not only the number of votes of money but the gobbledygook language in which they are couched. Even the present Minister of Public Works, for many years the President of the Treasury Board, was moved to say when appearing before a Senate finance committee last year that: "we are now getting to the point where the book is so thick and has so much in it that it almost appals people ..." and again: "The same problem with the public accounts which, over the years, have grown and grown . . . and now we have reached the stage where it is almost incomprehensible". That is what the minister said. It is one of the few really accurate statements he has made for some time.
An increasing amount of the estimates is made up of statutory items, that is to say, expenditures fixed by previous acts of parliament, and for all practical purposes beyond the reach of subsequent parliaments.
Another reason is the use of schemes such as dollar votes, legislative items, making commitments for a number of years ahead. Last year there was an item of $350 million in supplementary estimates for a public works program. It should have been in statute form and it was cnallenged in the other place, but it was passed
Estimates
because the minister produced an instant opinion from the Department of Justice which ran quite contrary to a Treasury Board manual which has been in existence for many years. Now that $350 million has disappeared into the cavernous belly of bureaucracy and probably will never be heard of again.
Another reason is the fact that the present Standing Orders and the previous decisions of Mr. Speaker make it almost impossible for the House to reduce the amount of any vote. Because of the limited amount of time and opportunity in special committees of the House for examining estimates and the method in past years of conducting the proceedings-most of these committees have been operating as kangaroo courts-members are inhibited in their tasks.
We have been left with a sort of comic opera atmosphere of contempt and disregard for the hard pressed taxpayer, and this is compounded when we consider the enormous acceleration of government expenditures over the last few years.
It is a fact the policy of expanding the monetary supply to accommodate these huge expenditures has been one of the principal domestic factors in the inflation which continues to ravage the average Canadian.
All of this would be bad enough if there were efficiency in the management of our accounts-the very fact that we are engaging in this exercise in the next few days is proof that this is not the case-and if in the larger context the Canadian government were, in fact, doing those things which ought to be done for the benefit of the people of Canada.
It was all very well when we were in an era of rising productivity, the rate of which did not lag too far behind the national accounts. But now, finally, the financial facts of life have caught up with the government which stands helpless and moribund, with no plan save only that of the modern king Canute, the Postmaster General, who says, "Don't talk about inflation and it will go away".
So here we are with expenses out of control; a governe-ment so big, so complex, that it is out of control, and this parliament is losing its right to challenge. The Auditor General's reports over the last few years pointed out over and over again that in fact we had lost the right to check properly and to restrain the government over public expenditures. I suppose we all have to bear some blame. Certainly members of parliament were delinquent in giving up the safeguards they surrendered. We are all responsible. None of us voted against those proposals.
The media have had very little to say about it. I noticed today that when the minister rose to speak about the estimates there was a general exodus of those who should be interested. I wonder if the situation will ever have enough political sex appeal to capture public attention. Certainly something is wrong but the public does not know' what.
There is another aspect which goes hand in hand with the question of control of spending. That is the right of the public, parliament and the media to receive adequate information from the government. I questioned the Prime

Estimates
Minister on this a few days ago and he gave me the usual slick, glib reply that the ground rules brought in by the former government House leader, which to some extent he said were imported from Sweden, these are quite ineffective. That is nonsense, Mr. Speaker. They have had no material effect on increasing the flow of information to members.
I had a chance to talk to the Prime Minister of Sweden, and asked him about what he had seen in this House and what is going on in Sweden. Out of politeness toward a distinguished visitor I will not pass on his comments, but he pointed out that in Sweden government information is within the full range of inspection of the media and the public. He said that a few days before he left three newspaper reporters went through his files for information. When will we get that sort of thing in this House, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When can we go through your files?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like the hon. member to see my files with all the complaints about what the government is doing to the people of Canada.
When the Prime Minister talked about Sweden he should know what the situation is there compared with Canada. We are away back in medieval days. Let us be honest, realistic, practical. Time has run out on us, and we are reaching the end of the road as far as being able to mount an effective parliamentary challenge to government spending in this House. We are a parliament which has lost its teeth, and we are being edged into a half baked presidential system without any of the safeguards which should be attached.
I am rather interested in the present desire of the Prime Minister to go to the British practice for some improvements. I would refer him to a book "The Passing of Parliament" by Professor G. W. Keeton. At page 33, the author comments:
Today, in Great Britain ... Transition would be easy, swift, and it could be accomplished with complete legality. Already so many steps have been taken in this direction ... Today, virtually our only remaining constitutional safeguard is the habit of tolerance and the existence of a powerful political opposition-
No wonder the Prime Minister is anxious to involve himself in the British practice.
What are the things that we need? We need the right to bring certain estimates, at the option of the opposition, into this House for full study in a revived committee of supply, with ample opportunity to question ministers. This is in addition to the continuation of standing committee examination. The estimates must be put in a form which is intelligible. We need to accelerate the examination of public accounts, and must have the right to have some examination in the House of public accounts committee reports. After all, when any animal makes a mess it should have its nose rubbed in it occasionally, and this is what should happen to the government.
The cabinet and bureaucrats must be compelled, under severe sanctions, to provide information requested. We must have the right to reduce the items of estimates, and all of this not just to prop up the prestige or enhance the dignity of the House but simply to do our job so that we can stand at the bridge and say to the government, "Your

estimates shall not pass until you have dealt with the grievances and the right to know of the people." Will we get it? I do not know. Certainly the bureaucracy will not voluntarily give up its authority, and the cabinet is made up mainly of recycled bureaucrats.
Today I fear there is not much hope that the House as a whole will go along with my suggestion because the government has a majority. Its supporters are quite satisfied with the scheme of things and most of them look ahead to the day when they, too, may have their chance to move up to the throne and become ministers and experience the great thrill of throwing around hundreds of millions of dollars of other people's money.
This leaves the opposition, or those of the opposition who will dig in and fight, and perhaps some in the media who may also perceive the dangers which threaten. Will that be enough to stimulate public outcry for changes? There is nothing certain about it, but we have to try because it is our duty, because there is not much time left, and because if there is any further increase in executive power the Prime Minister's office and the cabinet will shortly become, in legal form, what it is now in substance, a collective autocracy, with no restraints between elections.
The question I often ask myself, and I am sure others do also, is this: do people really want a continuation of the parliamentary democratic system or are they content with the executive dictatorship we have been building in Canada over the last eight or ten years? On balance I am convinced the great majority of people have a sound instinct, realize what is best for them and prefer the democratic structure which would permit them, through their representatives, to challenge the juggernaut of government.
So it is our duty to seek improvement, to say to the government which probably will not listen, and to the people who may, that this House, this parliament, must be equipped with the means and the tools to carry out its responsibilities. Society to live, to survive, to progress must change, conform and adopt.
The choice we face is either to secure these changes by the proper interrelationship of parliament and government so that from time to time we reach a consensus to bring the greatest good for the greatest number-a result which has to be judged by the needs of the people and not the wishes of the executive-or else we will have to cope with the painful alternative of explosive violence which we see around us. Mr. Chairman, the choice is for us in this parliament today.

Mr. Chairman, in the inter-party discussions which we had, we arranged for a certain number of departments to be given our attention during these three days. It is correct that the estimates of the Treasury Board were to be first on the list so that we could have a parliamentary discussion on government spending in general, and on the way in which parliament handles the government's estimates.
The hon. member for Peace River has conformed to that arrangement. I wish to make a few comments on what he
October 23, 1974

has said and on the things that have been designated for this discussion. I think it is fair to say we do not intend to stay very long on this subject. Rather, we welcome this opportunity afforded to us in these three days to get at the substance of the estimates of several departments. Accordingly, before long we will be into the estimates of the Department of Transport.
However, the remarks of my good friend from Peace River prompt me to make a few comments I had not planned to make. If I may be so presumptuous, I shall characterize his speech as being divided into two main parts. On the one hand, he levelled an attack at government spending generally. In fact, he called the estimates a $25 billion rip-off of the Canadian people. On the other hand, he criticized the methods by which we allegedly scrutinize the estimates or study the spending program of the government. One of my reasons for separating his speech into those two parts is that I do not want to confuse them. I want to speak about them separately.
With regard to government spending generally, I know that it is a favourite indoor sport to attack governments for expenditures, and to treat governments as though they are highwaymen holding up the Canadian people for the benefit of those who happen to sit on the treasury benches.
Let me say that I am terribly aware, and I have been around here long enough to have that awareness fully developed, of wasteful expenditure on the part of the government. I am frequently annoyed at the high salaries that are paid in certain areas. I am critical, as are all my colleagues, of government priorities in spending. Far too often unimportant things get the money that should be going into things that would make life better for human beings as individuals.
Having said that, let me deny the assertion that taxing and spending of the people's money is somehow a rip-off by highway robbers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. In order to make the hon. member's task easier and let him devote his time to that area which I think is more subject to attack, may I say I did not intend to create the impression that there was a challenge against all government spending. I was going back to my days in law when theft was defined as taking without colour of right. I was challenging the government for taking money without being subject to the usual precautions, scrutiny and safeguards which we ought to have. I ask the hon. member to take that as my understanding.

Mr. Chairman, I am quite prepared to let the hon. member put that gloss on what he said if he wishes to do so. However, the fact is he did say this is not properly called an appropriation of funds but a misappropriation. He applied that to the whole book. He said it was a $25 billion rip-off of the Canadian people. I want to make the proposition that this is an attack on government itself. It is an attack on civilization.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

My friends do not seem to realize that civilization does not consist of a
Estimates
lot of individuals living in a dog eat dog fashion. Civilization consists of an organized society in which we decide, in an organized way, how we are going to distribute the wealth that we produce. If we did not have government, if we were an unorganized conglomeration with each of us going his own way, poverty and suffering in this country would be worse than they are at present. Inequality would be far greater.
By having government, which is an organization of society, we see to it that at least a portion of the wealth we produce-and I mean real wealth, goods and services-is distributed among the people of the community as a whole.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!
If my friends to my right are hurt, they can say so. They can use the rest of these three days to bring out those antediluvian ideas that they want to put forward.
Hear, hear!

I submit that the major portion of the money-not just the 57 per cent, but the money spent on highways, defence, postal services, health and all the rest of it-that is collected by governments at all levels, municipal, provincial and federal, then recycled and spent, is a process of society deciding how our wealth is going to be distributed, and trying to do it on the basis of some sort of fairness and equality for all our people.
I insist that my friends to the right cannot stand up and call for massive reductions in government expenditures unless they say where those reductions are to take place.
Hear, hear!

Are they going to reduce the money spent on old age pensions? For my part, I want to see a lot more spent on old age pensions, family allowances, housing, health and all those services that will make life better for the Canadian people. I want to see less money spent on a lot of public buildings that are not necessary. I want to see a lot less money spent on high salaries. I do not want any more money wasted on us. I want the money we collect and recycle through the process of government to get through to the people.
I submit that this attack on government spending which we get from my friends to the right all the time is completely out of touch with the basic philosophy and basic fact of civilization. I once read an article, I forget where, which was addressed to Governor Reagan of California. The article said that Governor Reagan must be told that civilization costs money.
If we are going to have a civilized Canada in which people have health services, housing, pensions and an organized community which they can count on having some dependability, it is going to cost money. That is what government is all about, and that is true at the local municipal level, at the provincial level and at the federal level.

October 23, 1974
Estimates
People sometimes take the attitude that taxes are some sort of a fine, penalty, highway robbery or, to use the hon. member's word, misappropriation. I submit they are very often collected unfairly. A lot of tax is collected for wasteful expenditures and things that ought not to have priority-
Like the Senate.

Yes, like the Senate. Get that on the record. The basic fact is that we are, in this collective way, paying for services. When we pay taxes we are not paying a fine to the Minister of Finance, the President of the Treasury Board or anyone else over there. We are paying for the cost of services that government provides.
In the context of that, I claim full right to be critical of the way these moneys are spent. I claim full right to be critical of high salaries for top senior civil servants, members of parliament, and of other ways moneys are spent.
Speak of Barrett in B.C.

I am just as critical of any government, even if of my party's persuasion, that does it. I am especially critical of the failure to make substantial increases in the basic old age pensions, to spend more money on housing, or to provide other services that our people so sorely need. I believe in civilization. I believe in Canada being a modern, humane civilization. But I accept the fact that this will cost money, and the big corporations, the ones that are getting 60 per cent or 80 per cent increase in profits every year, aren't going to do it.
The money can be collected and used to provide for a decent civilization only if we do it through the instrument of government. I think we could have a much better government than the one we see opposite, but the fact remains that if we are to have civilization we need a government which is prepared to levy taxes and then to use those taxes on the basis of proper priorities to create a decent, humane society for all our people. So I urge that we not waste time on this nonsense of picking up this book of $25 billion dollars worth of estimates for the year and saying that it is a misappropriation act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is just a rip-off.

The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is more responsible than that. I know, because he is my friend and I like him. He could make a much better contribution to the debate than that. Don't worry about this talk about a minority parliament as opposed to a majority parliament. Whatever the situation, we have the right to try to make parliament work, and we want to see it work for the best kind of civilization we can have.
He is trying for a Senate seat.

If that remark has gone on the record, the member who made it knows there is one member here who would absolutely refuse to
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).)
go to the other place and it is this member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I have more sympathy with the hon. member for Peace River when he is talking about the other subject he dealt with, the question whether or not in parliament we give adequate scrutiny to the estimates. I do not believe we do. However, I still feel it is not much help for one side to damn the other because we haven't got a proper system. I believe we should put our collective minds together and try to work out a better system of handling the estimates, instead of just letting the opposition berate the government because we don't have it.
I have been around here for a while. I happened to come when the House of Commons was still handling estimates the way they were handled in the year one, and even though that was in wartime when we had a huge appropriation bill, it worked. We did every estimate of the federal government on the floor of this chamber in committee of supply, and of all the systems in my experience I think it was the best. The reason it had to go was because of the sheer explosion of expenditure. At the beginning of World War II the budget amounted to about half a billion dollars. In the first years after the war it got up to one or two billion dollars. I remember those terrible budgets which the father of the hon. member for Mississauga brought in-four or five billion dollars. Now it is $25 billion dollars. And with all the different things we spend money on, all the different things parliament is involved in, it was just impossible to continue the system we had down into the forties and fifties.
I was also here in the days when we did estimates on the floor of the House but had a limited number of days for them. That was just about as bad. In fact, it was worse. We got the estimates passed, but all the ministers had to do was just to sit them out. They knew that with the passage of time their estimates would get through. So we agreed, all of us in all parties, to try a new system of referring the estimates to committee. Then we bring them back to the House and normally we don't have this kind of debate- we just vote on them. I don't think it is working as it should.
I don't suggest we go back to the other system because there aren't enough days in which to do it, but I still think there is merit in the idea that at least some departments of the government-and here I am with the hon. member for Peace River, my good friend, 100 per cent-namely, the departments the opposition chooses, every year should be brought on the floor of the House and discussed without time limit.
I would rather have two or three departments in a year without time limit, than have 20 departments with two or three days each. The moment one places a time limit on estimates all the minister in charge of a department has to do is to sit there and listen to the speeches knowing that when the time comes the vote takes place and, with a majority government, his estimates will go through.
Therefore, I argue we should improve upon the present system, let most of the estimates go to committees as they now do, and let the members of those committees make the searching inquiries they talk about. But I think the opposition should have the right to say that we want these departments, A, B and C, or X, Y and Z, back here on the
October 23, 1974

floor. The opposition should pick them, they should come back to the House of Commons, and they should be discussed on the floor of the House of Commons without time limit. Unless something like this is done the so-called studies we make are not studies at all.
In this sense I do not blame the hon. member for Peace River for feeling we are just a rubber stamp approving something which has already been done. The size of that book, of course is frightening. It is at least four times the size of the book of estimates we had when I first came here, and it gives about one-quarter of the information. Surely some improvement can be made in his area in improving the handling of the estimates. I think what should be done is for all of us to put our ideas into the pot to see whether we can come up with some better way. Mr. Chairman, I believe we can.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make rather brief remarks after those made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien).
Since this is the first time we deal with a matter involving him, I would like first of all to congratulate him for his appointment as President of the Treasury Board. With his long cabinet experience and that spirit of his, I think he will be able to make a useful contribution.
Mr. Chairman, I also want to assure him of our full cooperation in the consideration of bills introduced by him but, of course, as long as they are acceptable to us.
When the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) was interviewed on Lise Payette's television program on the CBC, in Montreal, he said that his role was to limit, control and supervise the estimates of each department. He gave the impression that he coordinated the activities of departments and that the Treasury Board accepted to vote credits at the request of the deparment and established priorities.
Indeed, in the statement about the purpose of his department contained in the main estimates, it is said that the minister is responsible for the selection of programs and projects that will achieve the objectives of the government in the most effective manner and in accordance with its priorities.
Mr. Chairman, if I am not mistaken, and I would like to restrict my comments to this point, the minister is responsible not only for accepting a list of priorities established by the Cabinet, but also for applying it and coordinating it with the activities of other departments.
Mr. Chairman, if this is true, I believe that the minister will have much to do to modernize this department. His role will be to ensure that there will be no double funding to meet the same objectives and that there is no conflict between two programs, since, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said in the same spirit, it would be dishonest to blame the government for spending too much while requesting more money for other programs. But this does not mean, Mr. Chairman, that we should waste public funds in some areas because we allow double investments or conflicts between programs.
I would like to clarify this point by giving a specific example: Of course, these problems do not occur at the
Estimates
level of government leadership, but when the laws are applied in practice, Mr. Chairman, many of the criticisms made by our fellow citizens in this area are quite justified. The administration of the laws and the various programs cost a lot of money and do not meet the desired objectives. All public servants in general, except of course those whose working contract was being negotiated at the time, received $500 as a sort of bonus. Even the employees of Crown corporations have received this bonus. Yet, Mr. Chairman, the House of Commons staff did not get it.
Here is what I am driving at. When we get in touch with the responsible people in the manpower mobility program, we are told that House of Commons employees, being members of the civil service are not entitled to the manpower mobility allowance. On the other hand, House of Commons employees who request equal treatment with the civil service are told by Treasury Board or I don't know who that they are not entitled to it because they are not members of the civil service.
Mr. Chairman, this is the kind of inconsistencies which I think important to raise now when we are considering the estimates of the Treasury Board Department. The way I understand the minister's explanations, both outside and inside the House, the role of his department is extremely important. The responsible minister should set up within the Treasury Board a body that would look into such discrepancies that cannot be justified.
You have the choice of two things, Mr. Chairman: either House of Commons employees belong to the public service and, as such, are entitled to all its avantages, or they do not belong to the public service and are therefore entitled to all the benefits available under the various departmental programs, including manpower mobility.
I suggest that we should clarify problems such as this, so that our employees, wherever they are in Canada, or the Canadian people may get what is coming to them without prejudice or contradiction on the part of other departments.
In this connection, I should like to give another example. In the estimates of the department, we shall be asked to votre some amounts of money for the Opportunities for Youth program or the summer student employment program. Mr. Chairman, I feel these programs are important. They should come under the Department of Manpower and Immigration. It was a long time the responsibility of the Secretary of State.
For practical purposes, we may wonder, when we consider some projects, whether they were set up to create jobs to help municipalities or teaching institutions. Mr. Chairman, this is another example among many others of an instance in which the Treasury Board might have an important part to play. If, on the one hand, the minister is endowed with the necessary authority to allocate funds to various programs according to government priorities, I should imagine that, on the other hand, that authority of his to allocate funds should entitle him to review their enforcement. I should think the Treasury Board is a kind of watchdog on the look out for the proper enforcement of laws and the proper management of programs and public funds.

October 23, 1974
Estimates
If the minister manages the $27 billion paid by taxpayers and under various tax programs, I think he is responsible to the people for the proper allocation of those funds with the slightest possible amount of clashes between various programs.
I should therefore be glad to hear the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board in this regard, concerning that increasingly important part to be played by the department. I think the Treasury Board has a privileged position not only to coordinate the work of departments and ensure the enforcement of governmental priorities, but also to enforce laws, and above all to avoid useless and sometimes shocking and unfair contradictions as regards their enforcement.
Mr. Chairman, we in this House often vote for the allocation of sizeable amounts to some particular program. But when it comes to the practical use they are put to owing to ever more complex regulations as well as to civil servants who may feel overly secure in their job and also possibly arrogant and a long way from administration, it appears that those laws do not really meet the needs they were supposed to.
Mr. Chairman, I think the Treasury Board has a part to play, and it should have some organization responsible to the President of the Treasury Board for ensuring that the laws that are voted on and passed by the representatives of the people are being applied in conformity with their targets.
Mr. Chairman, to go one step further in that direction, if an hon. member were critical about something, before he would start pouring out his endless lamentations to the House and wasting the time of hon. members, he could immediately get in touch with the department concerned which would check into the matter of his criticism.
Mr. Chairman, I think that would be a guarantee for the public that the funds will be well spent and will serve their purpose. Nobody is happy to pay taxes, yet everyone has to, because that is the way the administration works. It is understood that the government must keep an open mind on all suggestions and positive remarks that might be made. I think one of those suggestions would be that the Treasury Board stop being run has it has always been, i.e. according to that good old British method where nothing moves and we are content with granting the funds asked for, and that, furthermore, it play an innovative role within the administration. Only then will the new President of the Treasury Board really prove equal to his task.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. gentleman from Peace River, particularly to his criticism of the way in which supply had been handled and his plea to go back to the good old days. In the good old days there was a natural termination to supply in the House of Commons; basically the population was rural in nature and people wanted to leave the House of Commons to get back to the farm to plant their seeds. Therefore, there was a natural desire to get the blazes out of here and do something constructive, so that the estimates usually passed.
Just before I came to the House of Commons in 1965 I had spent two years as an executive assistant watching

the House of Commons, particularly the supply procedures. I recall the good old days when we used to go through the annual procedure of voting supply just prior to the running out of the estimates. There was the odd occasion when, by accident, the estimates were not voted and the pension cheques would be held up for a time. Everyone would feel sorry, and the first opportunity they got they very contritely voted supply as quickly as possible.
The reason that we changed the supply procedures was that it was obvious that they were not working to the satisfaction of either the opposition or members of the government. Thus we came with the new system, the implications of which we are working our way through still.
Just what is the situation? We abolished the committee of supply and put the estimates in the hands of some 20 odd standing committees. At a stroke more time was made available for the discussion of supply than had been the case before. At a stroke there was a greater opportunity to question and to put on the griddle the administrators of government programs-that is, the civil servants. We never had that opportunity before.
We have more opportunity, as a consequence of the new system, to participate in constructive criticism of the spending policies of the government. There is more opportunity given to backbenchers to make themselves heard. Much more careful examination is permitted.
Mr.Baldwin: What about the Minister of Energy who won't let civil servants speak without his consent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All I can say to that is that any minister who allows a civil servant to express policy is clearly out of his mind.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say anything about policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If a minister has confidence in his civil servants he can certainly let them talk about administration, and this has been the practice for a very long time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Look at the record.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have always done that. At any committee I have attended civil servants appeared and provided information at the request of the minister. We still have the doctrine of ministerial responsibility in relation to what goes on in the department. That is the responsibility of the minister, and I see no contradiction at all. Indeed, I would say that the day we cease to have ministerial responsibility and a minister is not accountable for what goes on in his department, that is the day parliamentary democracy goes down the drain. I think the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is quite correct in his approach.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Do you agree with Macdonald?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say we still have the doctrine of ministerial responsibility, and if I were a minister I would be clearly out of my mind-

You are.
October 23, 1974

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: -if I allowed somebody else to take on the responsibility for which I, in the end, would be taken to task.
Look what happened to Stanley. They pulled the plug.
Oh, oh!
And look what happened to Herb Gray.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To go back to a more interesting subject, I think I am fair in interpreting the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River by suggesting that he is prepared to enter into discussions with those of us on this side who are interested in reform not only of the procedures of the committee of supply, but also the procedures of the House as a whole.
The essential difficulty we face is that we have had tremendous misallocation of the use of our time. We changed the situation because there are extraordinarily few members of parliament who now seriously seek to cut estimates. There are few members of parliament who really are serious about chopping items out of the estimates. Just take a look at any of the question periods since we have come back and you will find it very difficult to demonstrate, to any fair-minded person, that the thrust of the questions is for the government to stop spending. The burden of the questions generally is on why are we not spending more. With these changes we are spenders.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As the House of Commons we are spenders. If you will take a look at the estimates over the last two years you will see that that parliament, as a minority, was the greatest spending parliament this country has ever known, and it was a spending parliament in large part because of the minority situation. I cannot recall one instance in respect of any program that there was opposition by the official opposition, and in respect of which it voted against it.
The point is that the philosophy of members of parliament when it comes to dealing with supply has changed. We are no longer out to cut spending, rather we are out to increase supply. That means the approach we take in dealing with estimates is obviously of a different nature. It means that the old system we had was obsolete, and was properly thrown out, Mr. Chairman.
The present system of supply is not satisfactory to the government. The government would like to see substantial changes. The government feels that the opportunities the opposition has had to cross-examine in respect of estimates, both in the committees and in the House, have not been exploited to the full. It is our feeling that the 25 allotted days the opposition has now have not been utilized to the fullest extent, particularly in cross-examining on the estimates. They have been used for other purposes, not in opposition to the rules, but it seems that members of the opposition have had the opportunity within their grasp to focus more clearly on government spending if they had chosen to use the opportunity.
Estimates
After the estimates are returned to the House on May 31 there are up to 13 opposition days at the disposal of the opposition during the month of June. Do we see the members of the opposition bringing forth departmental estimates for discussion in the House of Commons? I suggest the answer is that we do not. Do we hear the opposition members coming forward and saying they agree to a special order in respect of the Committee of the Whole so they can bring these departmental extimates in here? I suggest we do not. Instead what we see is a never ending number of resolutions about this thing or that thing, all items of interest to the public, I am sure, but none that deal with supply.
Under the rules there are opportunities available to members of the opposition which they are not now using. If they were to think about the problem and come up with propositions I am sure the government would be more than prepared to go half way in accommodating them. They might suggest some kind of system to bring back to the floor of the House the estimates within the existing structure. I do not think I am saying anything new to members of the House of Commons because, obviously, this is the case stated by the present President of the Privy Council and his predecessor.
Let me deal with the matter of guidelines and the information the hon. member for Peace River mentioned and about which he is so concerned. I quite agree it has been 18 months since the guidelines were released to the House of Commons. They were referred to the Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, headed by an hon. member of the opposition and a member from the Senate. There was no consideration given during the last parliament to these guidelines which, as I say, were referred 18 months ago.
The point I am trying to make is that the government is prepared to do everything possible to co-operate with the committee. We are prepared to enter into negotiations with members of the opposition once the report is made. We want to ensure that members of parliament get all the information they require.
You mean all the information that Keith Davey won't let us have.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We are prepared to do everything we can to see that this comes about, but you cannot fault the government for not having referred these guidelines to a committee of the House of Commons which had the power to hold hearings, to call ministers and other witnesses, and produce a report over a period of 18 months. That is why this will be on the order paper again, and that is why it will be referred again to committee.
The government has been prepared to move quicker on parliamentary reform than have members of the opposition in many cases. The last point I want to make relates to the pro forma speech by the hon. member for Peace River in which he commented about remarks of the President of the Treasury Board. If the argument is not made by that hon. member it is made by the hon. member for Yukon, but the argument is always made, and it is always that they have not had sufficient time. They always say they are under the guillotine, and that these estimates are

October 23, 1974
Estimates
being forced down their throats. They always resent this very much.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are right on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Even when we had the good old days of the committee of supply opposition members still made the same speech. Nothing has changed. The point I am trying to make is that the circumstances may have changed but the argument has not. This is the same old gang with the same old thoughts.
What we obviously need is to work out some system so the estimates of government can be thoroughly investigated as quickly as possible. There must also at some time be an agreement to put the motion, however brutal that thought may be. This has always been the great problem, getting members on the other side to agree to put the motion. They have always had the concept that as long as they can spin out debate then nothing will happen. Then, of course, we are forced into the situation where some restraint has to be put on, and that has been the case in the past because of the mockery that has been made of supply procedures.
It seems to me that whatever new system of supply we come up with, we will still have to face up to the fact that at some point there has to be a decision. The government is the biggest spender of money and has the most people dependent upon it. We just cannot have a kind of system where things are left to the whims of a few people sitting in the House of Commons.
Members of parliament have a right to vote on these estimates. They have the right to vote against them, and they have the right to reduce them. If the present procedures are not adequate perhaps we should be looking for procedures to make sure their right is fully enshrined, so that if anybody feels he does not have the right this would set him straight.
I can recall the last time members of the opposition swiftly moved to cut into the estimates of a department. That was when they moved to cut out the expenditure of $19,000 in the estimates of Information Canada. The money had already been spent by that time. That is an indication of the opposition being able to cut out certain estimates. The power is there, but whether it is exercised is a matter for members on the other side to determine.
There is also the power on the part of members of committees to reduce estimates and to have these estimates come back in the form of a report. Members of a committee have the power to bring that report to the attention of the House of Commons. That has never been done, to my knowledge, in the manner prescribed by Standing Order 58 by any opposition member of any standing committee. I may not be completely correct on that because I believe once in a committee they went after the president of the CBC and reduced an item to $1 at the time the hon. member for Cochrane was chairman of the committee.
My own feeling is that the current procedures in dealing with supply, while an improvement over what we had before, can still be improved. I do not think we can look at

the question of supply in isolation. I think it must be considered in relation to the over-all procedure of the House of Commons.
There is no secret about the fact that the workload of the House of Commons is increasing because of the amount of government legislation which is before the House. We have, therefore, limited time before us in the House to deal with matters of supply. These are very knotty problems, and it seems to me that if members opposite wish to bring back to the House the committee of supply, in addition to the 25 days now allotted to them under standing orders, then there must be a serious overall attempt to speed up the legislative process.
We have not yet faced the basic problem that our workload is expanding while the time frame remains the same. We will have to make some very difficult decisions.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to spend very much time speaking about things referred to specifically by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, except to say it has been my good fortune to serve as Leader of the Opposition in more than one legislature.
I notice here, as well as where I served before, that members on the government side who have never served in the opposition tend to have a certain glibness. I might even say they tend to have a certain arrogance. I know only one cure for this; that is for them to have the good fortune to spend a certain amount of time in the opposition.
I first came to this chamber in the fall of 1967. At that time the estimates came before the House, but there was a time limit. Having come from a legislature in which ministers had to answer questions if they hoped to get their estimates passed, and a legislature in which it was possible even for a small opposition to force a minister to give a satisfactory and full answer, and where the government really was responsible to the legislature and through the legislature to the people, it was very trying to come here and find that the ministers did not answer questions, and that there seemed to be absolutely no way to get ministers to answer questions.
I can recall being completely amazed when sitting here to notice that a minister would say he would take note of a question and then, when it suited him, he would get up and answer the question to which he chose to reply. No matter how unsatisfactory his answer may have been there was nothing the opposition could do about it under the rules as they existed. Today of course there is even less capacity for the opposition to make the minister really responsible.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River spoke about the minister rather than the public servants being responsible. Of course that is true. The point I wish to make, however, which there is no need to belabour, is that we no longer have responsible government in this country.
Oh, oh!

Excuse me. Let me finish. We no longer have it in the sense that a minister must answer to this House. There is no way I know, at least in a majority parliament, for a minister to be made to respond in this
October 23, 1974

House. I wish members of this House and the people of the country to think about this.
I shall not argue this afternoon about the amount of the expenditures, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred. That is not my concern this afternoon. My concern is to emphasize that I was personally struck by the situation here, having come from a legislature in which a minister had to answer questions satisfactorily if he wished to get his estimates through. Dealing with supply is not just a matter of dealing with estimates.
The refusal of parliament to pass supply traditionally has been a weapon available to parliament. In the old days it was used against the King, and then in modern times against a minister. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River must get through his head the fact that it is not merely a matter of reducing estimates, although that might be important. The essence of consideration of supply is that really this is the moment of truth. That is what it used to be, and should be. That is the time when a minister really must answer to this House. In my time here a minister has not had to do this, and on very few occasions has done so. In that very real sense I say that we no longer have responsible government at the federal level in this country.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is nonsense.
If the minister had listened to what I said-

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did carefully.

-he would have to agree with what I said, because there is no way under present circumstances in which a minister can be forced to give information to this House. A minister does not give information unless it suits his purpose.
In a sense I find myself in considerable agreement with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre although I do not know whether I would say he has necessarily put forward the right solution, that of bringing the estimates back to the House, since ministers did not give the information in the House except when it suited their convenience.
This is a very important question. I understand the concern of the government about getting more bills through the House, and so on. Although I understand this concern I would point out that there is a very important other side to the coin, which is that the system is not working. No one need kid himself. When I came here it was very apparent that a minister was not answerable to the House. He was not answerable then, and is not answerable now. There is no point in any one in this House pretending otherwise.

Mr. Chairman, when I asked if I might speak on the estimates I had no intention of becoming involved in the semantics of the rules. That is not my bag. Most of the remarks I had intended to make in reply to my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River were made more effectively than I could make them by the Leader of the Opposition.
Estimates
I should like to remind the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that I served as a minister in a majority parliament, and at that time my Prime Minister, no matter what the provocation, insisted that I stay in the House on a particular day for as long as it took to give the minority every chance to protest. He held that the more vigorous the opposition might be, the more tolerant government should be in allowing it to protest. I do not believe the hon. member for Timiskaming is in the House at the present time, but I have taken his attack four times in the same speech, delivered four times on the same day. Perhaps I could remind the parliamentary secretary, who was not there at the time, that in those days the NDP only had eight members.
Good old days.

And the official opposition had less than 50. Those eight members in the NDP would get together and plan their two or three days' attack on the estimates, and they did more to stand the government on its head than did the less than 50 Liberals because they understood the pressure that could be put on a minister who had to stay here until they were satisfied. One of the reasons why the government from 1958 to 1962 was one of the best governments in this country was the calibre of the intelligent opposition we got from the NDP.
Hear, hear!

I pay them that tribute to illustrate a point.
I have been back now in the House for two years, and I confess that I am seriously ashamed and shocked that even though I try to be constructive on occasions and not always partisan I have been in committees where we tried to obtain information from ministers and their officials, but where the Liberals, of whom there were only eight, were not contributing anything much in particular yet each took his full ten minutes so as to make sure we did not have time to ask our questions. This is not a violent statement of prejudice. Now that they have the majority I see the difference already. All that the members on the Liberal side do at the meetings which I have attended in the last two weeks is to vote against us.
Naturally we are going to accept the offer of the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. We do have to try, because we are all good Canadians, to find how we can make it work a little better. I do not foresee bringing all the departments here, and keeping them here indefinitely until the opposition is satisfied, but I would suggest, as a non expert, that if we had in the opposition the right to pick two or three departments, and the government ministers did not know which were going to be picked, then all the ministers would be a little more willing to reply. If we had the right to pick the worst offenders, we would be able to straighten things out. It would not be perfect, but it would help.
We want to try to make parliament work better. Certainly the rules were bad in my day, but they are worse today. That is the point.

October 23, 1974
Estimates
As an example of the other type of abuse of the estimates let me make use of the right of members of parliament to ask questions on specific details. If I could attract the attention of the President of the Treasury Board for a minute, I have a specific question to ask him. When the estimates are prepared on supplementaries, has the custom changed, namely, that these estimates are a true indication of the estimated cost of the item for the fiscal year named on the cover of the estimates?
The answer is yes, Mr. Chairman.

The
minister says yes. That is where I think I can demonstrate to him that we can serve this parliament and country well. If we turn to page 6 of the supplementary estimates for Energy, Mines and Resources, we note that there are two supplementary estimates. Vote 11a is for $470 million. In committee we questioned the minister and found that this item was up to the end of October, and that we did not have the information we required for the approval of that estimate in the committee.
But in questioning the minister, and from his own opening statement, we find that Vote 52a for $330 million only covers the months of November and December. Therefore my submission to the minister is that this is not a true reflection of the cost, and that parliament and the people should be told what will be paid in the forum of this subsidy for oil in eastern Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes.
This parliament, before it can vote these estimates sincerely and honestly, must know that there is another estimate of approximately $300 million, if not $400 million. I will not quarrel as to whether or not this is the exact figure. The fact is that these estimates do not cover the full fiscal year. Purely on the grounds of a technical error or, as the hon. member for Peace River would say, sloppiness, we are not getting a true estimate.
Naturally one asks why this is so, and the rationalization given to us in committee was that this whole subsidy has no legal basis. Therefore, since they are acting illegally in collecting this money, they did not want this illegality to last too long. They hope, some time in this parliament, to get a bill passed that would legalize the illegal act. I suggest that once you lose your virginity, the time factor is unimportant.
I ask the minister this question: will he consider, in consultation with his officials-because members of the opposition have no right to do this-whether the estimate now before this House, before these three days are over, could be raised to something approaching more closely the real estimate of the cost that the people of Canada will have to put up for this subsidy. I suggest, using the information with which the minister has provided us, that the subsidy to the eastern people is costing us $100 million a month. If we add another $300 million we will have a more accurate estimate. Can the minister tell us whether it is possible to make this change?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to reply to the honourable member in clarification of that item. I referred

to this problem in my presentation. Of course in the supplementary estimates I have tried to cover the months of November and December. It is because this process of transferring money for the export of oil to the eastern consumer has been debated in the House a long time ago. The bill was introduced in the House, but was not passed because of the election. Now we are in October. We started the session only a few weeks ago. At the start we had the debate on the Speech from the Throne. To be honest, we do not know when the bill will be passed. We have made a guess, but we cannot take into account all the factors.
Normally, this bill should be passed by the end of the year, but as we wanted to have the authority to spend that money before the end of the year we put that in the supplementary estimates so that, before we make the expenditure, members of the House will have the occasion to debate it and vote on it. If those estimates are passed by the end of this week the House will have authorized the government to pay the subsidy to the eastern consumers until the end of the year. We hope that by that time the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will have received approval through the passage of the legislation in the House.
If the House turns down the legislation, it will mean that at the end of the year there will be no more authority to pay the subsidy. We are not trying to mislead anyone. On the contrary, we are making sure that hon. members are aware of the fact that those payments will be made in November and December.

Mr. Chairman, I think we have joined issue fairly on this item. My point is that the government has no right in the first instance to assume that parliament will pass this legislation before Christmas. The government knows that all parties have supported the principle of this subsidy. We are not quarrelling about the fact that they are doing this illegally because of the circumstances. We are saying that the proper presentation to the House and to the country of supplementary estimates A, and the calculation of the estimated cost, whether done legally or illegally, is not the point. It should be the amount you expect to spend by the end of the fiscal year, not the calendar year.
I am raising this point for the experts because I do not consider myself an expert. I recall that when I sat in Treasury Board we always hounded the departments to be precise in their estimates. If a minister brought before Treasury Board estimates for eight or nine months, he was sent back. I am really asking the minister if he would not agree that to add $400 million would be more honest estimating and more honest reporting to the House. The media should be able to report to the country that this program is going to cost $1,200 million, not $800 million. This matter is put forward without any desire on my part to make political hay, but just in a desire for honest reporting. If the officials can find a way to do it, let them be a little more honest in reporting their estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to look into that question. I have been very candid and explained why we did this. We could have estimated up to the end of the fiscal year, but we took a calculated risk that the bill
October 23, 1974

would be passed by the end of the year and we did not want to presume too much regarding the content of the bill. It was and I regret to use the term, a conservative estimate and we tried not to prejudge what the House would do. The point made by the hon. member is a good one, and perhaps we should forecast for the total fiscal year. I wanted to be as honest as possible with the House. I did not want to hide anything; I wanted the judgment of the House when members voted on the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. At this time I should like to seek direction from members of the committee. It was suggested that the time allocated to the consideration of the estimates of the Department of the Treasury Board should be a maximum of an hour and a half. Three or four members are standing, seeking to speak. Much time has been spent in general debate on the question of past and future procedures for the study of supply, so I would invite comments from hon. members on how the Chair should proceed at this time. Should we close this debate, and proceed to another item?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, possibly there are a few comments to be made and questions to be asked. The committee might consider allowing this department's estimates to continue to not later than 5.30. That would leave three hours for consideration of the estimates of the Department of Transport. I know the minister is most anxious to get started.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would go along with the suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River. To a large extent, these proceedings are in the hands of the opposition. It was their suggestion that time be allocated to the departments, and if they would like to have less time for the Department of Transport, and more for Treasury Board, I am sure we will be satisfied.

Mr. Chairman, since we are operating on the basis of an agreement and not a fixed order, obviously we have to be a bit flexible. My colleagues and I would rather move to Transport now, but we will accept, say, 5.20. That is, if this department is not finished by 5.20, we will move on to Transport.

Mr. Chairman, on the same point of order, as the previous speakers pointed out, it is not a rigid regulation. It is rather an amicable arrangement. I think I will support the proposition made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with the hope that the President of the Privy Council may accept it. Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity, still on that same point of order, to say to the parliamentary secretary that if what he said a few moments ago about the opposition was true, Mr. Chairman, we would have answered no a long time ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are proceeding under an agreement, and this makes it a little more difficult for the Chair to meet the objective of 5.20 or 5.30. Hon. members, of course, could cut short their speeches or questioning so that as many members as possible could participate.
Estimates

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I do not know what the agreement is that hon. members are speaking of, but I was not privy to it. I think I have as much right as anyone else in this committee to speak and to be heard. I am getting a little fed up, because I come into the House day after day and find that the party "wheels" and party whips have got together and made some sort of agreement. I represent a good many constituents in the province of New Brunswick, and I desire to be heard and I hope to be heard.
Go ahead.
I do not belong to any of the standing committees and therefore do not have an opportunity to speak in those committees, so I want to be heard in this House and in committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I note that the hon. member, like other hon. members, rose and participated in this debate. Some hon. members have not yet been recognized. It is the prerogative of the Chair to call on hon. members one at a time; two members cannot speak at the same time. We have to proceed in an orderly way in committee of the whole and in the House. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta.
