Mr. Chairman, I had not planned to speak at this point in the proceedings, but when the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River made his eloquent speech I thought we had, suddenly, a TV camera in the House. The hon. member said the opposition has the right to vote on estimates, to vote against them or to reduce them; but, Mr. Chairman, hon. members on this side of the House do not always have a chance to get answers in committee.
The other night I had the misfortune of attending a committee meeting on supply and services when the minister was sick. I understand he is still sick. However, he was represented at the committee by his deputy minister. The president of two corporations was before the committee-Canadian Arsenals Corporation and Canadian Commercial Corporation. I agree that if we had been given proper information and our questions had been answered, we would have no reason to raise these matters in this chamber. I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River should make the same admission as some members of his party who were at the committee: they were ashamed of the answers we were getting. The president of Canadian Commercial Corporation could not tell us the names of the ten major companies with whom he dealt, and as president of Canadian Arsenals Corporation-it is the same gentleman-he could not answer all the questions we asked. In fact, he could not answer any. I made a motion which even the Liberals supported, that we demand this information.
I think the government should make sure that the civil servants who come to committees are prepared to answer the questions of the opposition. I think if any government member or any minister went through the report of that committee meeting he would not find one question that was unfair. Every question was legitimate. Canadian Arsenals Corporation has been losing money for a year. Although it employs 500 people, it is costing the Canadian taxpayer $3 Vi million. Therefore, the Canadian people have a right to know what that company does in its

October 23, 1974
Estimates
operations. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River shakes his head. We could not get answers.
I am standing here now taking up time of this committee, which I did not plan to do. I have to do it because I listened to what the hon. member said, which sort of indicated he is white and we are all black. I do not think that is quite the way it is. If he is looking for co-operation, he should make sure we get the answers we want. He should also make sure that the people who appear before the committee have the answers we want. Members on this side of the House would then co-operate with members on the other side and make sure government business is handled quickly.

Mr. Chairman, like other members, I did not intend to intervene. This has been a very useful debate on how estimates are handled. I understand that in the British parliament and in other parliaments they have almost given up on the estimates. I believe in many cases the estimates are tabled. That is an abdication of the responsibility of parliament. There is legitimate concern on the part of members of the opposition who have expressed their point of view about their ability to deal with the estimates. The difficulty lies in the fact that as far as estimates are concerned, the committee system is not functioning the way it should. The chairmen of committees should call more frequent meetings to deal with specific situations. The time given to committees has not been adequate to deal with the witnesses brought before them. Hon. members of this House, myself included, have not been adequately prepared when going to committee meetings. We have not been prepared to the extent necessary in order to make the examination that it is our obligation to make.
The reform of the procedures of this House wherein we abolished the committee of supply was, on balance of consideration by hon. members, a good move. The rules provide for better use of our opportunities of examination. However, there is an obligation on all of us who are members of committees to make sure that meetings are more frequent and to make better use of the time allocated for witnesses and civil servants who are called before committees. If there were less waste of time and more efficient and adequate opportunity, we would carry out the kind of examination that I am sure we in conscience feel we should.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to direct some questions to the President of the Treasury Board. When the President of the Treasury Board appeared before the miscellaneous estimates committee and answered questions, I tried to get some rationale from him as to the formula used by the government to control increasing expenditures at the federal level. At that time he said the goal of the government is that total federal expenditures in relation to the gross national product should be relatively the same. He then said they have been relatively the same, and gave certain figures. For example, government expenditures in 1972 represented 15 per cent of the gross national product. He also referred to certain other years. I pressed the minister on that point and said I understood the figure was more like 20 per cent. I gave him some
(Mr. Reynolds.]
figures. Then there was general agreement that he would supply a table, which would be appended to the minutes of the committee meeting, setting out his figures.
That table has just appeared. It seems to seriously misrepresent the government's position and I take great exception to the way the table is set out. For example, it shows 1973 total government expenditures, and then in small type, "exclusive of transfers to other governments, at $17,595,000,000". Surely the President of the Treasury Board knows that the estimates being considered at the present time are $24 billion.
There is no explanation whatsoever for that figure. The, various percentage figures are shown. However, when they come down to provincial and municipal figures, an entirely different presentation is made. The impression left is that federal government expenditures, before all transfers, are much lower in reality when compared to the provinces that are shown. I would like the President of the Treasury Board to explain why they have to practice such deceit.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to reply to the argument of the hon. member. When I appeared before the committee I tabled the information which I had. I did not want to mislead anyone. I offered not only what I was stating, but the table that I had in front of me. One can, of course, argue what is and what is not a real government expenditure. Sometimes in the total expenditures of the three levels of government there could be double accounting. I wanted to make sure that did not happen. I am not an accountant, but I know what is a double entry. If we take $1 billion from the taxpayers at the federal level and transfer it to the provincial government, it is the same money; it is not new money. One sees the same $1 billion in our expenditures and in the books of the various provinces. It is not a new expenditure that must be taken into account.
I would like the hon. member for York-Simcoe to tell me if I am wrong when I try to explain to the people-and the people have the right to know-that in relation to the gross national product of this country, total federal expenditures has not increased over the last ten years.
Wrong.

The hon. member can say it is wrong, but I have given the table to the House. That is his opinion. However, most of the increase in public expenditures at this time has occurred at the provincial level. Many expenditures of the government are often transfer payments to the provinces to help them fulfil their obligations. It is important that the public knows that the federal government transfers money. However, it is not right if the taxpayer believes that twice the amount of money is being spent, when in fact it is just being transferred to the provincial governments. The public is given the wrong impression when that is included as double accounting. I have tried to explain that. Of course, the hon. member is at liberty to disagree with me. Sometimes I am very happy when a member like him disagrees with me. However, we must state the facts.
If you exclude the transfer of payments from the expenditures of the federal government to date, they are no
October 23, 1974

higher than 12 years ago when related to the gross national product. In addition, we must look at the number of new services that we have given to the public. The public should realize that. That is why I have given these figures. I am surprised that the hon. member is not repeating the figures I gave in relation to what was the consideration in 1961-62 when the take of the federal government from the taxpayer, in relation to the gross national product, was higher than it is today, despite the fact that we have introduced new programs. We have tripled family allowances, we have new programs for old age security, health services and other services for which the people of Canada are very appreciative. Despite that, the take of the gross national product is no higher at the present time.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, it is in the interests of this committee that we get the facts. I am referring to total government expenditures before all transfers. Does the minister agree it is approximately $24 billion and that that is something in excess of 20 per cent of our gross national product?

I have the table here. Total federal government expenditure, including transport, is $22.4 billion-18.8 per cent of the gross national product. That compares with $7.1 million and 18.1 per cent in 1961 at a time when there was no medicare, no health services, no family allowances at the level we have now. So I think that for one-seventh of one per cent of the GNP we have done very well in the last ten years.
Hear, hear!
Does the minister not think, then-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister and the hon. member are in disagreement, but because of the limitation on our time I think I should call on other members. There are only seven minutes left.
I understood one could speak for a 20 minute period, or ask questions for a 20 minute period.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The order says members would be allowed to speak once for 20 minutes once. This would not exclude the asking of questions. But as hon. members know, the debate has been twofold, it has been on the general question of supply, and we have already taken a good deal of the time which should have been allotted for the consideration of the Minister's estimates. The Chair cannot control what hon. members say, and when I suggested that the time allotted to this particular phase of the debate be extended, it was in order to allow as many members as possible to make comments on the minister's estimates or to ask questions.
If we pursue a line of questioning between the minister and the hon. member because they base their arguments on different figures or have different points of view, the time allotted to this portion of the debate will be used up. That is why I thought it would be fair to call on other hon. members. If there are a few minutes left at the end we may come back to the hon. member for York-Simcoe.
Estimates

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to get into this disease of verbosity on inflation which has been rendered here this afternoon. I have three questions I wish to direct to the President of the Treasury Board. On page 29 of Schedule A there is an item which reads: "contingencies, $90 million dollars." Then, in small print, it says:
-and authority to re-use any sums allotted for non-paylist requirements and repaid to this appropriation from other appropriations.
I should like an explanation of what that means.
My second question concerns an item on the same page under "public service bilingualism." I should like to know whether this represents the total cost of bilingualism in the public service and agencies of government and, in particular, whether it includes the amount voted for the Commissioner of Official Languages.
The third question I should like to ask concerns employer contributions to employee pension programs. How much of this is for the Canada Pension Plan and how much for the Quebec Pension Plan? I thought those were the type of questions we should be asking at this time, Mr. Chairman, and I will appreciate specific answers to the specific points I have raised.

I will give the hon. member some specific answers. First, when we take money from the contingency vote in the fiscal year for one department, as the time comes for supplementary estimates we put that amount into the supplementary estimates so that hon. members may have the chance to comment and vote on the expenditure which has been made. As to the second question, the answer is, no. Not all the costs are included. I think it will take a couple of minutes to get the answer to the hon. member's third question. I will give it to the hon. member later in our discussion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Could the minister tell us whether last summer a directive was sent by Treasury Board to all government departments to the effect that no federal property should be offered for sale in any circumstances? Does this apply even to buildings which are not being used, and which are not likely to be used by the government in the foreseeable future. I am thinking, for example, of post offices in towns in which new post offices have been constructed.

The policy is this: when a building is not used by the government it is turned over to the Department of Public Works to determine what kind of use the government might have for it in the future. If the department finds there is nobody within the government who has any use for the building, I believe it is turned over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for disposal. Until the Department of Public Works has determined the government has no other use for the building, it is not prudent for the government to sell it, since it might well be needed for another operation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
This does not appear to be the performance that is taking place in Exeter. The answer the minister has given me saying the building would be offered to other government departments is not adequate in this case, because an offer has been made to lease to the town a building in which the town is interested. However, the

October 23, 1974
Estimates
town wishes to purchase the building. Possibly the minister could obtain a further answer for me later.
Yes, I think the hon. member might be able to get an answer later from the Minister of Public Works, who will be presenting his estimates in due course.

Perhaps I might turn to another part of the minister's testimony before the committee. I asked him to what extent had provision been made in the accounting for the promises which had been made during the Liberal election campaign. The President of the Privy Council replied:
I think we will only implement $10 million in new money for that out of a budget of $22 billion.
Will the minister give us details about this $10 million?

What I said at the time was that only $10 million had been approved for new programs up to that date. The amount of $10 million had been allocated to certain programs which had been mentioned by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs during the campaign.
The political party of which I am a member has made other promises and the government will implement them in due course. We have stated that we will do this and that, and take four years to live up to our mandate. We have said: "Don't worry about it, we will live up to our obligations".

With the House's consent, Mr. Chairman, I would like to give an answer to the third point in the question put by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones), relating to the contribution to the federal government pension plan and to the Quebec provincial pension plan. I must say that we do not have any information on the subject and consequently we cannot say how much money has been contributed to the province of Quebec and how much money has been contributed to the Canada Pension Plan general funds; but what we can say is that the total for the 1974-75 fiscal year is about $32 million. The hon. member can find the details page 28.

speechtext: Order. The committee will now proceed to the consideration of the estimates found in Schedule A of the bill on pages 25, 26, 27 and 28.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that after all the discussions and questions we have now had in the House, I am ready to answer, with the help of the officials of the Department of Transport, the question hon. members wish to ask with regard to the estimates of that department. I therefore need not make a speech: I would doubtless repeat what I will say during the debate on those estimates. I am therefore at the service of the House to answer questions.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to emulate the minister and not make a speech. I should like to make a few remarks for four or five minutes, and save some of my time for later and for my hon. friends. It is with a great deal of respect that I say that in the more than 90 days since July 8 we have seen encompassed therein not a 90 day decision period, as the late Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson once promised, but 90 days of indecision. Nowhere has this been more clearly manifested than in the Department of Transport. Commitments made by the minister and his predecessor dating back to the twenty-eighth parliament have not yet been kept, and promises and undertakings, proclaimed with much fanfare during the recent election campaign this summer, have so far amounted to nothing.
This vast, sprawling Department of Transport-again I say this with respect-runs the minister; the minister does not run the department. I think this is a regrettable situation. We in the official opposition favour certain definite policies designed to improve the Canadian transportation system and which we believe are necessary clearly to establish and assert the authority of the minister. We should like to see the minister take some initiatives to
October 23, 1974

exert his authority, which we believe he has pursuant to legislation that already exists.
I refer the minister to a statement made by the President of the Canadian Transportation Commission at our most recent meeting of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. He said that he agreed that, pursuant to section 50 of the National Transportation Act, the minister could, if he wished, use the CTC as an instrument to direct the railways to change some of the unsatisfactory practices that now exist.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the hon. member referred to the testimony of the President of the CTC. Would he please be kind enough to quote the page, because I did not understand him to say exactly what the hon. member said.

Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, I do not have, nor do I believe exist, the minutes of that meeting. I do not wish to be unfair in this regard, and perhaps I have misquoted what the president said. I checked with my hon. friend from Regina-Lake Centre a few moments ago to see whether my information was correct, and he seemed to agree.
I only wish to point out, Mr. Chairman, that it is my understanding that parliament has provided several ordinary standards of efficiency that a railway ought to meet. For example, the Railway Act requires that a railway company shall, according to its powers, without delay and with due care and diligence, receive, carry and deliver all traffic offered for carriage on the railway. That provision is in section 262(1) (c) of the act. There are other sections, for example section 265(1) and (2), which require that a railway company shall, according to its powers, afford to all persons and companies all reasonable and proper facilities for the receiving, forwarding and delivery of traffic.
These requirements or conditions are mandatory and if the railway does not meet them it is derogatory in its duty. It is pursuant to this type of reasoning that the power of the minister, under Section 48 of the Transportation Act, provides that the commission shall upon the request of the minister inquire into, hear and determine any matter or thing that under the Railway Act it may inquire into, hear and determine.
I would take the minister one step further, again back to Section 50 of the Transportation Act, and say that the government in council having decided on its own motion that the railway is insufficient or unsafe, from some point of view or other, has the power under the act to refer that insufficiency to the commission for action, and the commission must comply immediately with the government's reference. I only bring this forward to express the hope, in a constructive way, that the minister will explore the options available to him under the existing legislation.
Going back to March 14, 1972, the minister's predecessor, the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, made a commitment that he would be bringing in important legislation, among other things designed to reconstitute Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation, divorcing it as it were from the CNR, and introducing a Canadian National Railways Act, and other legislation
Estimates
covering the Railway Act. This was promised in the twenty-eighth parliament and it has not been done as yet. I suggest to the minister that for that reason he can hardly blame us for being a little skeptical. That is why I put this suggestion forward at this time. If he is not going to bring forward some new initiatives he should at least explore the options he has open to him.
I think the minister should, as a major initiative, try to improve labour relations and encourage discussions between labour and management under the auspices of the Department of Labour. I know he will have read the story in today's Globe and Mail under the heading "Rail unions bargaining may produce 1975 formula for settlements". The article goes on to refer to improved labour negotiations in transportation in the upcoming year, and refers also to airlines. I suggest that the minister should work toward this objective. He should seriously explore the objective of having labour contracts for our two major railways expire at different times. This would help to avoid national paralysis at times of labour disputes in this industry.
I believe the minister should work seriously toward establishing Crown agencies, divorced from the CNR system, to operate the ferry services to our island provinces. We would not then get into the same type of problem we have experienced during times of national disruption of our rail service.
I would also suggest to the minister in the context of these estimates that, in the interest of increased transportation, safety, and free dissemination of information, he should insist that in any accident investigation carried out by the CTC, the minister's department or other investigative bodies, the results should be accessible to the public. This has not always been done, but 1 think the minister agrees it should be done.
I notice that the latest information dated October 21, the federal-provincial ministers' communique on western transportation initiatives, relates that the minister also stated this would be followed at a later stage by an information act that would seek to make available the broader range of transportation information that is needed to plan and realize Canada's transportation needs.
I would hope that the minister in this context will try to make certain that the activities of our Crown corporations are more accessible to the public, including the specific duties and responsibilities of officials employed therein. I make these suggestions in all good faith to the minister.
I should now like to ask the minister a few questions through you, Mr. Chairman. My first questions concern the STOL program, and I would refer to the statement the minister made to the standing committee in April of this year. The minister said there was $15.5 million budgeted for the buying of aircraft and for the STOL operation in Montreal and Ottawa. I believe there has been an increase of about $10 million, bringing that to the level of about $25 million. I realize these are only approximate figures.
I am troubled by the allegation, as I think the minister is as well, of Mr. Ian D. Sinclair, Chairman of Canadian Pacific, in which he forecast a higher level of expenditure, claiming that if all the costs of the STOL operation are considered the total cost would be $158 million, not $25
670

October 23, 1974

million as government spokesmen have contended. I would like to stop now and ask the minister to tell us briefly by how much Mr. Sinclair's estimate is in error.
$125 million.

The minister is then saying that there is absolutely no relevance or accuracy in that estimate of $158 million. I thank the minister for that answer. I should now like to ask him some questions about marine transportation. The minister has been quoted as being in favour of a Canadian merchant marine, or the restoration of the same. Can he tell us whether his department is considering seriously the establishment of a Canadian deep sea merchant fleet as requested by many shipping concerns and, in the labour movement, by the Seafarers' International Union?
In the context of that question I should like to ask the minister to comment on the action of the CPR in the commissioning of seven large ships to be constructed in Japan, and registered outside Canada in order to avoid Canadian taxes and the hiring of Canadian seamen. Is the minister aware that these ships are engaged in the transportation of Canadian natural resources, which probably helped pay for their construction in the first place?

Mr. Chairman, we are at grips with a problem here. The hon. member might perhaps tell me exactly what the situation is. The shipyards have now received orders for the construction of a large number of ships.
Some of them, such as Davie Shipbuilding Limited and Marine Industries Limited of Sorel, and probably several others, have contract for years to come. Even if Canadian Pacific were to decide tomorrow to award a contract, let us say, to Marine Industries Limited, it could not expect to have it completed before three or four years.
The problem for shipyards throughout the world in the last few years has been the large number of contracts.

Why do we have as many contracts in our shipbuilding yards in Canada? I suggest it is because all the shipyards in the world are operating at full capacity and they cannot fulfil any new orders. Unless the hon. member can prove that CP has done this because it wanted to discriminate against Canadian shipyards, I can only believe it has done so because it could not have the ships built in Canadian shipyards.

That may well be the case, and I thank the minister for his answer. I know of one or two shipyards that are perhaps not capable of building as large a vessel as CP requires, but they would be very glad of some government assistance in upgrading their facilities and their capabilities. The minister will have to look into this aspect as well if he is serious about increasing our capability in the merchant marine field.
I have a related question which I put to the minister at a recent committee meeting. I would like to ask him about the terms of reference and the appointment of Mr. Desjardins, pursuant to Section 14(5) of the Pilotage Act, to enquire into the Laurentian Pilotage Authority. Now that

the minister has had an opportunity to consider this, would he indicate why the terms of reference or conditions read as they do, and indicate whether that is the case common to commissions of this type, or for some reason is this unique?
I refer to two conditions. The first is subclause 2 of the terms of reference. It states that Mr. Desjardins shall not be subject to the customary rules of evidence, nor need evidence be taken under oath. The second is that the investigation shall not be conducted by means of public hearings but, on the contrary, through the investigation and examination of those persons whom the said investigator deems possessed of evidence relevant to the subject matter whose evidence should be examined in the public interest.
This may be very innocuous, Mr. Chairman, but the terms of reference in respect of this particular appointment trouble me. I also wonder why a similar investigation of the pilotage authority was commissioned to Mr. A. F. Marler, whose report was received on December 31, 1973, I believe. Can the minister tell me why it was necessary to have two reports dealing with the same subject in such a comparatively short period of time? Could he also tell me whether or not he has decided to issue publicly the Desjardins report?

Well, as you know, the Desjardins report was not made under the Inquiries Act of Canada. Mr. Desjardins was asked by the Minister of Transport to prepare a report on the problem of language on the St. Lawrence River. This is the report we have. One might ask why this inquiry was not carried out in a different manner, or why a royal commission inquiry was not made into this matter. That would be an acceptable question. However, for the time being what we intended was to ask Mr. Desjardins to see what would be the impact of using both languages on the St. Lawrence River so far as pilotage and the duties of masters are concerned. This is the report we have.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for that answer. Perhaps I might return to another part of my question. I may be making too much out of the terms of reference of the investigation. It could be that this is a common thing. However, I still would like to know why Mr. Desjardins was directed to carry out the inquiry and waive the customary rules of evidence, including the requirement to swear in witnesses.
I would point out to the minister that although this is not under the Inquiries Act, as he rightfully pointed out, I believe it comes under the next section in the Pilotage Act, section 14(6), where it is specifically stated that in an inquiry such as that of Mr. Desjardins there are all the powers, pursuant to the Pilotage Act, which one finds in the Inquiries Act. For example, was this requirement exercised in respect of the Marler report, which I presume deals with the same subject matter? Perhaps the minister does not have that information handy.

No. I would like the hon. member to tell us whether he believes there are any shortcomings in respect of the mandate Mr. Desjardins
October 23, 1974

received. For instance, had he received another mandate would it be possible that there would be more light on the subject that was discussed? This is the only question. We do not mind under which act he functioned. Mr. Desjardins studied the problem of security of navigation on the St. Lawrence River. He produced a certain amount of testimony, which is very well specified in his report. I think what the hon. member should ask me is whether I am satisfied with that report, or whether we might have learned more had we used another means of inquiry.

Mr. Chairman, through you to the minister, may I say I am intrigued by this precisely for the reason I am unable to obtain information. Perhaps the minister will remember that a short time ago, after this parliament opened, he indicated he had the Desjardins report on his desk. Since it was so difficult to obtain I became interested in it because I understood it would be made available.
Before the standing committee the minister indicated that the Desjardins report would be made public, but I believe the minister was in error because he said later the same afternoon that there was not in fact a public release of the Desjardins report. I would like to make some constructive suggestions but I find it difficult to do so since I have not received a copy of the report.
As a lawyer I am bothered by the fact that any person who is to conduct an inquiry should be specifically forbidden to do certain things. For instance, I refer to the section which states that the investigation shall not be subject to the customary rules of evidence, nor need evidence be taken under oath. I do not think that is a very healthy type of prohibition in respect of anyone conducting an inquiry, particularly an inquiry into such an important subject as this. I do not wish to belabour the subject further because I know in due course I will receive answers and that the report will be released.
If I may, I should like to ask the minister whether he will seriously consider splitting off Air Canada from its financial inter-directorate dependency on the CNR? Does the minister have this in mind?
Yes. However, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if we should keep on the first aspect of this question. What is your problem? Is it the fact that you do not have the report?
This is not his problem. It is your problem. You are the minister.

I merely wish to understand exactly what the hon. member wants. If the only problem is that he wishes to have the report, then I do not think I could refuse circulation of the report. Once he had that report he could ask his questions. Would that be all right? Now perhaps we might switch to the other point. What about Air Canada?
Is it your intention to split Air Canada from its dependency on the CNR?

That is a very important question. I am ready to discuss that, either in the committee or in the House. If one were to ask my opinion I would
Estimates
say that, personally, I would like to see Air Canada one day disassociated from the CNR. However, at the present time it is not. Would this be a good thing? I would like to have your opinion on that. My own view is that I would like Air Canada to be separated from the CNR.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member for Central Nova but the time allotted him has expired. I shall now recognize the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.

There are a number of matters which I, and other members, would like the minister to explain, if he can do so this afternoon or tomorrow. I will repeat what I have said every year for six years. I wish there were a great deal more in the supplementary estimates and the main estimates each year so that the Canadian Pacific Railways, their subsidiary and ancillary operations, could be placed under public ownership to develop a publicly owned and operated air, ground and water transportation system which would in fact meet the needs of this country.
Similarly, we need more estimates to re-nationalize the CNR, especially when I read some of the remarks of the new president about making profits, etc. He sounds as bad as the president of CPR. This is another reason why we do not get the kind of service from our ground and air transportation systems to which the public is entitled.
In fact Canada and the U.S. are about the only two countries left in the world that are still hiding their heads in the sand and relying on the nineteenth century concept of private enterprise profit making transportation systems. Even the Minister of Transport has admitted-I am not saying that I will quote him directly but I think I am paraphrasing him reasonably accurately-that competition between railroads in Canada does not work. I could not agree more. It may work for railroads, but it does not work for Canada and its people.
While there may not be very much of anything in these supplementary estimates to start accomplishing the things I have mentioned, I hope that after what the minister and his predecessor have been through at the hands of our railway systems, our airlines and a few other transportation systems in Canada, he will now persuade his colleagues, and get the government behind a program to place our transportation systems under social ownership so as to meet the social and economic needs of the country.
There are also a few current matters that have presented problems in parts of Canada, and I know the minister has been conscientiously trying to deal with them. I may disagree with the methods he used, but at least I give him credit for trying to do something about them. He has not had too much success as yet. I am referring to such things as rail branch abandonment, freight rate freezes, and cost disclosures from the railroads, to name three of many items that have concerned both him, us, and several provinces for some years. I hope that after I sit down, shortly after eight o'clock, the minister will take a few minutes to try to bring all the members of the House up to date in these areas.

For example, if the minister will recall-and if not I will refresh his memory-I believe there was a public commitment from the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board that no branch lines will be abandoned without the concurrence of the provincial government. However, I have the impression that the minister is now saying that no lines will be abandoned until suitable alternative arrangements have been made. I am sure there are at least three provinces which do not know which of the two is correct.
If the minister is correct, what does he mean by "suitable alternative arrangements"? Can he tell us about his meetings with his counterparts from the three or four western provinces in the past week in this regard? What is the federal position? Can we rely on the commitment we obtained prior to the election date? Will the minister consider extending the rail branch line freeze, at least until we get all the information that is needed from the railroads regarding their costs, and regarding the wishes of the users of the rail service along those branch lines, the farm and business organizations concerned, and the municipal and provincial governments concerned?
I agree that some rationalizing is needed, but not nearly as much as the railroads would like, and not nearly as much as the people who would like to get into the commercial trucking of grain would like. What progress is the minister making in this area? Will the freeze be lifted at the end of the year? How many lines are to be abandoned, and under what conditions? What kind of suitable rates does he envisage? What progress is he making in this whole area.
With regard to the freeze on the freight rates I should like to know from the minister how much money has been expended so far in compensating both railroads for the freight rates in the past 15 months, or for whatever length of time the freeze has been in effect. A figure has been given to me but I do not know whether it is accurate, and I should like the minister to tell us how much compensation has been paid to the two major railroads, whether any of it is in the supplementary estimates, and how much is in the new main estimates. I should like to know on what basis such compensation payments are made. Is it on the basis of a telephone call from Mr. Sinclair saying: "We need so much money to compensate us for the freight rates", or does the minister have accurate information regarding the necessary compensation to bring the railroads up at least to a break even point, if not a profit point, on the freight rates that were frozen?
I hope that a blank cheque has not been provided to the two major railways by way of compensation for the freight rates. Will the minister extend the freeze on freight rates? The freeze only affects rates on about 22 per cent of railway traffic, and there is a large area of other rates with which they have been having a ball.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The Minister of Transport will be along in a few seconds. In the meantime, we could perhaps carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at six o'clock, the committee was considering the estimates of the Department of Transport. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.

Madam Chairman, I think the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley is a great fellow, but even he does not measure up as a substitute for the Minister of Transport who we have been waiting to question for a number of days. At the time of the supper adjournment I was speaking about the freight rate freeze. I would ask the minister to spend ten minutes or so answering the questions that I put before six o'clock and those I am going to ask now, and to deal with some statements I intend to make.
I asked him before six o'clock what amount of compensation the government is paying to the railways as a result of the freight rate freeze. I want to know from the minister whether any compensation was paid during the freeze. The railways raised rates on commodities on which the rates were not frozen in excess of any justifiable increase in cost, in order to ensure they did not close during the period of the freight rate freeze. I am interested in knowing what inquiries the minister has made about this, and what he has to say to the management of both railway companies in terms of freight rate increases during the so-called freeze.
I have a table somewhere here on freight rates that were not affected by the freeze but which, in fact, were increased. To add insult to injury in western Canada-but I will have to forget that, Madam Chairman, because I cannot find it. Suffice it to say that for steel products shipped from Hamilton to Calgary, compared with steel products shipped from Hamilton to Vancouver, both railways raised their rates in February and March. They are still doing very nicely.
An hon Member: Here comes the minister.
Excuse me, I was delayed by a Conservative.

It is too bad the minister did not do like me tonight, watch his waistline and not eat too much.
I hope, Madam Chairman, you will grant me an extra couple of minutes to repeat what I have just said. I was talking about the freight rate freeze. I would like the minister to advise whether he inquired into rate increases by the railways during the freeze on rates. I am thinking particularly of steel products being shipped from Hamilton to Vancouver, Hamilton to Calgary and so forth. There are a number of similar instances such as rapeseed versus rapeseed oil from Nipawin, Saskatchewan, to Vancouver. I understand it is still cheaper to send the rapeseed by rail to Vancouver and boat to Japan, than to end the oil to
October 23, 1974

Saskatoon. I hope I am wrong. Possibly the minister has made inquiries into that. Was this pursued in his discussions with the representatives of the four western provinces?
I now wish to deal with a subject which angered the minister and about which he waxed eloquent in this House some time ago. I refer to cost disclosures. If the railways were not prepared voluntarily to disclose their alleged costs, the minister said he would require them to do that even if it was necessary to involve parliament. We all applauded. The minister was assured that that kink of legislation would be passed in record time. In fact, if it will make him feel better, I will not make a speech.
My understanding, from what limited information I am able to get, is that the four western premiers and the Minister of Transport are still being treated like a prospective customer of the CNR or CPR when it comes to getting information. We would like to know the minister's intentions with respect to when he will be bringing that legislation into this chamber, either as an amendment to the Railway Act, Canadian Pacific Railway Act, or whatever act needs to be amended. The railroads should be required to make full disclosure of the cost estimates they use to arrive at what they call justifiable returns on freight rates. We are anxious to know that.
I now wish to return to the subject of branch lines. In his discussions with representatives of the western provinces over the past several days, did the minister deal with the other side of the coin; the social, economic and human costs versus the savings, convenience and profits for railways and trucking companies with respect to what number of branch lines, if any, are to be abandoned?
Last May and June a branch line 90 miles in length was closed. I cite this as an example of the kinds of costs people face in order to convenience the railroads and grain companies. Because a branch line had not been operating for over three months, a farmer in Imperial, Saskatchewan, was told he would have to deliver his carload of barley to Davidson, 35 miles away. This involved 10 loads and an additional $300 in order to fill his quota and get a special permit from the Canadian Wheat Board. He asked why he could not deliver his grain to Watrous as that was on the CNR main line. He was told he could not do that, and that he had to deliver to Davidson.
The estimates will be coming up to provide for the maintenance and operation of branch lines of both railroads. I hate to say this about my pet publicly owned transportation system, the CNR, but both railroads have deliberately allowed their branch lines to deteriorate to the point where no one would touch them with a 10-foot pole. I hope the minister will not fall into the trap of taking over the roadbeds and trackage because it would cost upwards of $1 billion to put them into a condition to carry traffic.
We would like the minister to report on extending the freeze on branch lines. Will he live up to the commitment made by his colleague, the Minister of Justice, that no branch line will be closed without the consent of the provincial government? If that commitment is to be forgotten, what does he mean by "an appropriate alternate method of service"?
Estimates
I particularly want to know how much money the minister and his colleagues have agreed to part with by way of compensation during the freight rate freeze. If the minister is unable to give that figure now, I hope he will do so during the question period later this week or next week. Remarks were made earlier today about ministers answering questions in a straightforward manner in order to ensure that the opposition do not keep debate going because they are not getting answers.
May I remind the minister that he, like some operations in his department, cannot continue to try and be both fish and fowl. We need to have a transportation system that is operated as a public utility, publicly owned and controlled. We do not want any of these half measures of transportation systems that are part private and part public, both trying to operate for profit, both trying to provide service which is better, and "never the twain shall meet".
The minister and the government must make up their minds one way or the other. They cannot continue trying to be half pregnant. It is either a publicly owned and operated transportation system, integrated and efficient, with service getting priority over profits, or it is an undertaking in the private sphere looking for all the fast bucks it can get. Even if the minister does not want to adopt all the solutions I am asking for, if he will agree to start off with CP Air Lines, we shall support him.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Madam Chairman, I had the good fortune, last week, of meeting the ministers of transport for the western provinces; we discussed the problem of prices, which were frozen for some categories of goods, and also that of the railway companies which have also been frozen for a certain length of time, that is till the end of 1974.
In both cases, I said that this matter had yet to be decided by the federal cabinet who took the initial decisions. The matter will be taken up very soon, this week or next.
Unfortunately, I cannot tell the hon. member this evening whether prices will continue to be frozen or not.

October 23, 1974

In any event, I believe we will soon reach a decision, because time is running out. The matter is on our agenda. [English]
I told the transport ministers of the west that they did not have to take a decision, because the first decision was taken by the federal government and not by the transport ministers of British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. So we intend to take this decision, rightly or wrongly. At this moment I am not in a position to tell the hon. member exactly what we are going to do.

A crystal-ball.

For 1973. But if you asked me how they arrived at that amount, my answer would be that I don't know.
I am not sure whether you have recognized me again, Madam Chairman. It was my understanding we were allowed 20 minutes. Have my 20 minutes expired?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Madam Chairman, the hon. member is not dishonest, but he is putting to me a question that he knows I cannot answer. The truckers did not ask for any compensation. The hon. member is not going to get an answer to that from me.
Oh, oh!

What do you want me to say?

You are not being serious. Let me tell the committee two things, if they will allow me

Madam Chairman, I think first I should answer the question put by the hon. member for Vegreville. The first question concerned the Crowsnest pass rates. Nobody indicated-certainly I did not-that we were going to modify that part. If ever we intend to do that, hon. members will have a formal proposal before them. Up till now, no one in my department, and certainly not in my office, indicated that we should modify the Crowsnest pass rates.
Having regard to the amendments to the National Transportation Act, of course, we intend to bring about some modification. I have discussed this matter with the ministers of transport from the west and I think we are close to agreement. That does not mean the problem will be solved in that way. These amendments will have to be brought before this House and discussed here. There are

problems, as hon. members know, and we are ready to discuss them here.
The third question had reference to boxcars. As hon. members know, we have instituted a monitoring system to find out exactly where the cars are, whether we have enough cars and how they are being moved. We had a conference last May in order to discover how many cars we actually had, if the number was sufficient and if the railways had plans to build enough cars to meet the need, we know very well that if the decision is to build more cars, it will be impossible to have them in service by December, January or February, and it would be childish to think otherwise. I think it will be perhaps a couple of years before we finally have all the cars we need.

As you know, through the Canadian Wheat Board we decided to have a certain number of hopper cars built. They will not be ready next winter; there is no doubt about that. If the hon. member can think of a way to have those cars delivered next winter perhaps he would tell me and I will apply it. There is no way to do it. We have given orders and have voted the money so that we will have the hopper cars we need to move the grain.
So you do not intend to do anything this winter?
We have done everything we could.
What else will you do for this winter?

What do you think I should
do?
Resign.

Madam Chairman, I do not wish to play politics. However, I asked a question of the minister a few moments ago and still would like to have an answer. I asked about the search initiators. I read a statement from the Canada Gazette. I would like an answer. What does the

minister know about the regulation which was supposed to be in effect for July 1 this year, and which still is not in effect? The minister has answered three other questions and I still have not had an answer to that question. I wish the minister would give me an answer. If he cannot tell me then he should say so and I will tell him all about it.
There are certain technical problems which we did not overcome. We are trying to solve them and will consider the situation.

I find it very hard to believe that the government has come across some technicalities it does not know how to solve. There are sufficient people in the gallery to solve the total problems of Canada. In Canada there are 1,460 tugs that are five tons or more. In the province of British Columbia there are 824. There are 430 in Canada of 15 tons or more and 170 of these are in British Columbia. I know the minister is aware that since 1958 there have been 41 wooden tugs sunk in Canada involving the loss of six lives. Since 1958 38 steel tugs have gone down involving the loss of 34 lives.
A total of 40 lives have been lost in the tugboat industry in Canada. This is one of the reasons the guild and the tugboat association have been pressing so hard to get this regulation in order to save the lives of others. I cannot understand the minister saying there is a technicality involved in this. Lucas Marine in British Columbia built a buoy which met all the qualifications of the regulation. They went into production on the basis of the fact that the government passed a regulation which was to be effective in July this year.
Because the government, through one of its people in the department, stated this is delayed for six months this company is sitting in British Columbia with buoys it cannot sell. It has nowhere to sell them because the major companies do not want to become involved in this expenditure in these circumstances. The president of the guild has demanded that the government put this regulation into effect for the safety of the tugboat operators and to save lives. While the government will not allow this regulation to come into effect we are risking lives.
In British Columbia this year a tug went down with a loss of three lives. I do not blame the minister for this. It is not his fault that the tug went down. However, if this tugboat had had the search initiator buoy on board it might have been found sooner, and certainly those lives could have been saved. I cannot understand why the minister does not know more about this serious problem.
I know representatives of the guild are planning to come to Ottawa sometime next week to plead with the minister to bring this regulation into effect immediately, and I hope he will say he will do that. Perhaps tonight he will stand up and tell this House and the country that, for the great benefit of the men and women working on tugboats, he will ensure that the regulation which the government passed will come into force immediately, especially in view of the fact that its taking effect is overdue since July 1. This is a very serious problem, but I have one other issue that I must mention before my time is up and I know that there are other members who have important questions.

speechtext:
Order, please. I have not been in the Chair for the first hour of this sitting but I should like to obtain some direction from the committee at this time.
On looking at the suggestions that were made by the President of the Privy Council I read on the second page that it is the agreement with respect to the debate that each member will be restricted to one twenty minute speech in committee on each department, but that this restriction would not apply in the case of direct questioning or answering, nor would a minister be prevented from rebutting points made during discussion.
The point I want to bring to the attention of the committee is whether I am to interpret this suggestion, or any other chairman of the committee is to interpret it as

allowing a member who does not take up the twenty minutes allotted to him for a speech to compensate for that time by a twenty minute questioning period. I think that we tried to clarify this a few minutes ago. I suggested to your predecessor in the chair that we were trying to follow an agreement rather than putting the Chairman on the spot where he would have to make a rather difficult ruling with regard to time. I think I am interpreting the President of the Privy Council correctly when I say that he agreed with the suggestion that the spirit of the rule was that the member speaking and asking questions could take up the full twenty minutes allowed him, provided the minister's time was not counted in replying. In other words, what difference does it make to the committee whether a member takes twenty minutes speaking or twenty minutes asking questions? I see the President of the Privy Council nodding his head. I think this was the understanding that he affirmed a few minutes ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
