Why don't you keep your mouth shut? I guarantee not too many members from British Columbia will stand up on this issue, but the tugboat owners will come down here wanting to see the problem solved.
Mr. Chairman, here is the telegram:
After serious consideration of all facts involved and view expressed the ministry is taken under review the extent of the application of the search initiator buoy regulations to tugs of more than five and not more than fifteen gross and this will be the subject of a circular letter to be forwarded within the next few days. It is considered that the dictate of safety require that existing regulations continue to be written to tugs of more than fifteen tons gross.
It is signed by R. Illing-I do not know who that is- MOT, Ottawa. I think that telegram proves that the minister is mistaken in what he just said. Those regulations are not in force. I am asking the minister why they are not in force and when they are going to be in force?
Mr. Chairman-
Bail him out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. minister rising on a question of privilege?
Just participating in the debate, Mr. Chairman.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, and with all due respect to the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond-Delta, as a member from British Columbia I have worked very closely all this time with members of the Canadian Merchant Service Guild on the west coast and made representations to the Department of Transport. They are well aware of the problem that we brought to their attention. As a matter of fact I just spoke to Captain Arnie Davis who is the Secretary-Treasury, and he indicated to me that the regulations are in force on the west coast.
Hear, hear!
No more headlines. It is a knockout.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should warn the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta about the disadvantage of raising arguments as a question of privilege. The hon. member might differ with the minister on all this and the answer which he got-I do not know any of the facts-proves that there is mainly a difference of opinion or interpretation. The hon. member who has the floor should use the floor to make his views known.
Mr. Chairman, I did not interrupt these proceedings on a question of privilege. It was the hon. member for Vancouver East.
No, you did.

I am sorry, but hon. members on the other side must realize I was using my 20 minutes and I was interrupted. I would say to the hon. member for Vancouver East that if he has been involved with this problem very seriously he must have had discussions with Captain Griff Morris, the Vice-President of the Canadian Merchant Service Guild. I had a meeting with him last Saturday. He pointed out this problem to me and said these regulations are not in force, and are not being enforced. I do not know where the hon. member got his information. All I can say is that he is mistaken.

Mr. Chairman, since spirits are beginning to run high, I would like to move from the Pacific to the Gulf of St. Lawrence where the water is somewhat colder.
Last year, I think, I asked the Minister of Transport about continued icebreaking service in the Gulf of St. Lawrence to provide safety for ships sailing the gulf and the area of Rimouski, and moving upstream from Quebec City to Montreal. At that time, the minister informed me that the question was under consideration and that a permanent icebreaker would be put in service, probably in 1974.
Is the minister in a position to inform the House whether a permanent icebreaker will indeed be put in service in the Gulf of St. Lawrence this winter, specially in the Rimouski, Les Escoumins and Saguenay areas, to provide increased safety for ships navigating those areas during winter months?
Does the minister intend to reply?
Does the minister want to answer my question? Did he understand it?

I did not fully understand the question, Mr. Chairman, because I was reading a document. I apologize, I thought he was talking about the Vancouver matter.
If the hon. member would like to repeat his question, I would be delighted to answer him if I can.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but the question seems to me to be easy to understand. Last year, I asked that a permanent icebreaker be put in service in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, Rimouski, Les Escoumins and Saguenay areas, and the minister replied that the matter was under
:



October 23, 1974

consideration and that eventually, in 1974-75, a permanent icebreaker would actually be put in service in those areas. Now there, is the minister in a position to tell the House whether there will eventually be an icebreaker next winter to offer relative safety for ships?

There are icebreakers in service in the Gulf of St. Lawrence as far as Quebec City and even Montreal throughout winter. Now, are there enought of them? Our problem comes from the fact that we are short of icebreakers. As a matter of fact, a number of them which are being built will help maintain navigation on the St. Lawrence River. However, I could not assure the hon. member that we will never be without icebreakers between Rimouski, Gaspe and Matane.

A supplementary question, Mr. Chairman.
Can the minister advise the House whether there are any icebreakers being built at the present time?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, there are two of them. There is also a project for the construction of a super icebreaker which should enter service within the next few years.

Mr. Chairman, for a while I did not know whether I would be able to speak tonight. I am certainly pleased to see such a large gallery. I did not think they would all turn out to hear someone from Churchill speak.
We have gone from the east coast to the west. We are now going into central Manitoba. I do not know whether many people realize there is an inland port called Churchill. The last ship of the season left Churchill at high tide approximately two hours ago. That was the twentieth ship to have visited Churchill this year.
Within the next few days the minister will probably issue a statement that some 22 million bushels of grain were hauled out of Churchill, an amount that is almost unsurpassed. Let me assure you, Mr. Chairman, that Churchill is capable of handling between 10 and 14 million bushels a month from July 15 to October 15. The reason the authorities do not handle that amount of grain is that they simply do not have the funds to keep the port in operating condition.
We see that approximately $12.5 million will be spent over the next four years to upgrade the port of Churchill. I can assure hon. members that this will only look after the maintenance of that port. What is the department doing to upgrade the facilities in Churchill so that at least 40 million bushels can be stored or shipped through that port? It is a very vital line of transportation in central Canada and the central United States. Can the minister give some answer to that?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I can give the hon. member an answer. The hon. member says we are only doing what is necessary to maintain the port of Churchill, keeping it open and operating efficiently. I regret to say that is not true. The government of Manitoba knows we are spending more than $12 million to improve the port of Churchill. At this moment the government of Manitoba is asking us to re-direct investment in order to
Estimates
increase even more the efficiency of the port. We agree, and we are doing that. Therefore, what the hon. member has said is not quite true.

Mr. Chairman, as an election promise the government said it would revamp the total grain handling system. I do not know if the minister knows where Churchill is, but it is one of the most important grain handling facilities in central Canada. The minister met with western ministers in Saskatoon. I have here a statement entitled "Progress towards the improvement of the port of Churchill and the development of the port of Prince Rupert".
I wish to refer to the blue book detailing the estimates. I see that for the port of Churchill, approximately $2 million is being spent. That is strictly maintenance money. How is the port of Churchill going to be developed, or is it just going to sit as it has for many years?
Very important also is the fact that the rail facilities into Churchill are such that there have been many train wrecks on the line. This holds up ships coming into the port. I understand the transport committee has promised $20 million for rebuilding the railway from Gillam to Churchill. Can the minister state where this is in the estimates and from where it will come?
Mr. Chairman, it is under normal CNR expenditures. What we said we would do for Churchill, we will do.
When?
We are doing it right now. When were you last in Churchill?
I might tell the minister I have been there many, many times when he has not been there.

Mr. Chairman, a few days ago I had discussions with a responsible minister from Manitoba, Mr. Evans. He agreed entirely with the procedures we are following. He is keenly interested in the development of the port of Churchill, and thinks we are making the right moves. He would, of course, like the process to be accelerated. We agreed entirely, and I must confess the provincial authorities seemed to be as interested as is the hon. member in the development of the port of Churchill. But they do not believe we can get rid of the ice 12 months a year. They know there are limitations, and we are trying to work within those limitations.

I am not really interested in trying to keep Churchill open for 12 months a year either. All I am saying is that the facilities which are there now ought to be utilized to their full capacity. What I know is happening is this: they are trying to develop the shipping of other commodities through Churchill and trying to stay away from grain. Yet the port of Churchill is ideal for the shipment of grain. The storage facilities are ideal. There is very little dampness up there; once it turns cold in the fall it stays cold right through the winter.
I sometimes sit and listen to people talk about the difficulties being experienced with the handling of grain

October 23, 1974
Estimates
on the east coast and the west coast. I can assure hon. members that in Churchill there is no need to worry about space in which to store grain. It is a big country up there. Also, grain need not all be moved up there in a great rush in the summer time. Grain could move there all through the winter, and then it could be stockpiled. If this were done we would not run into the trouble we experienced this summer when ships were lying in harbour waiting to load, and there were insufficient stocks on hand in Churchill though cars were backed up for 100 miles on the Hudson Bay Kailway. If these stocks had been moved up during the winter, supplies could have been built up and there would have been no difficulty whatsoever.
When the minister and his officials are talking about revamping the grain transport and handling system, let them not leave the port of Churchill out, because the port of Churchill is an important part of the economy of the north. The federal government has invested a lot of money in Churchill to revitalize the community. What is needed in an economic base to support the facilities which are presently there, and we should never forget that the presence of grain handling facilities in the north constitutes an ideal situation.
Regarding the railway I would suggest that one way of alleviating some of the tie-ups in the area would be to construct a passing rail between Gillam and Churchill. At present when trains are up to 155 cars long, it is impossible for the train to leave Churchill if there is a train going through Gillam. I hope some of the $20 million earmarked for the expansion of this railway will be spent in this way.

I propose to ask questions on certain specific matters in the course of my remarks, and I hope the minister will have an opportunity to answer them without getting involved in too much speech making. I am satisfied that now the hon. gentleman has had the opportunity of spending a couple of days in Saskatoon, with all those clear skies and fresh air, his thinking will be at its most acute and that, flanked as he is by two assistants from Saskatchewan, he will be able to answer my questions without hesitation.
We in western Canada are concerned about the reference in the Speech from the Throne to measures to speed up the movement of grain. However, the minister did not tell us about any concrete steps which are being taken or which are anticipated on the part of the government in respect to the more efficient movement of grain this winter. He did say that the construction of hopper cars was contemplated or, perhaps, that it was under way, but added that it would be around two years before they were delivered.
I directed a question on this subject to the minister responsible for the Wheat Board asking him what specific measures the government had in mind, but the hon. gentleman did not elaborate in the course of his reply. Thus I ask the Minister of Transport if he would give us an example, possibly just one example, of a step in the area of transportation which is currently being taken to facilitate the movement of grain this winter?

The only way in which I can answer that kind of question is by saying we shall do our utmost to ensure the movement of grain this winter. I
am no more in control of the future than is the hon. member, or even his leader. Many things can happen, but we shall work very hard to satisfy the farmers in the west. That is all I can say. Anything else would be either a lie or hypothetical.

To carry on with my 20 minute question period, may I bring to the attention of the minister the fact that according to authoritative evidence the snowplows used by the Canadian National are at least 30 years old and require replacement. Again I ask the minister whether there is even remote consideration being given to making any funds available for the purpose of providing equipment, in particular for replacing the snowplows to deal with the inevitable snowfalls which will be experienced in the course of deliveries to the west coast this winter? Has a request been made to the railways to consider upgrading this equipment?
I presume the hon. member reads the newspapers in the same way that I do, and I know that the CNR has ordered over $1 billion worth of rolling stock and equipment.
Any snowplows in that equipment?
I hope there are. If they don't do it I think we shall have to do it through this corporation we announced in the Speech from the Throne.

During the past three years when our markets have been exceptionally good-something for which we are all grateful-there has been delay for one reason or another in the delivery of grain because of the poor quality of the tracks and the inability of some of them to carry the rolling stock needed. Is the minister in a position to become involved, either by making representations to the railways or otherwise, in the solution of these difficulties? Can a statement be made with respect to the replacement of rails to bring them at least up to an acceptable standard?
I can tell the hon. member that I have been making representations to the railways for a few months now.

May I turn to matters of policy within the department as they relate to air transport, particularly in western Canada. I should like to make particular reference to the province of Saskatchewan, part of which I have the honour to represent. I should like to ask the minister about a press release following his meeting with the western transportation ministers in Saskatoon, who requested the minister to allow greater involvement and input by the provinces in regard to a bilateral air transportation agreement.
Would the minister consider instituting an international air service from the province of Saskatchewan? It seems to me that the province of Saskatchewan would welcome a bilateral air agreement so it could have air connection with the state of North Dakota, and with the city of Minot in particular.

October 23, 1974

I did discuss the question of negotiations with foreign countries regarding an air agreement with the ministers from Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia and Alberta. Our position was that it is difficult to integrate the provinces into the process of negotiation, but that we do try to take care of their interests. All of us in this House represent Canada, and the government does try to take care of the interests of each province. If we are not doing that, then perhaps we are going in the wrong direction.
With respect to the last agreement reached with the United States I am aware that Saskatchewan was not entirely satisfied, and we did make some modifications. On the other hand, Alberta was satisfied. There were some urgent needs there which had to be met.
I think the best way to deal with the matter is to have a meeting of ministers before negotiations commence, but once the negotiations are started I think the matter must be left to the federal government. I do not see how there can be any provincial involvement at that stage.

I thank the minister for that answer and I should just like to make one or two other brief inquiries concerning my province. May I ask the minister whether or not the government has given consideration to the great need in the province of Saskatchewan for development of air facilities, particularly in the northern part of the province? Once again we are embarking upon a very significant and substantial degree of uranium exploration and mining in the northern part of the province, and this calls for adequate air transportation to service the people of that region. There is a great need for navigational aids and air transport facilities to man this new industry in northern Saskatchewan.
The fact of the matter is that at the present time it is expedient to use the service from the city of Edmonton and Fort McMurray in Alberta. However, I think it is logical to request the minister to improve air transport facilities in the province of Saskatchewan. Will he give the committee an undertaking at this time that adequate consideration will be given to this rather modest request?

The hon. member is aware of what we are doing at the present time. I was in Saskatoon yesterday or the day before, I do not remember which, and some very substantial improvements are being made at Lac La Ronge. We are concerned about improving air transport facilities in Saskatchewan. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is satisfied with what we are doing in that province.

Mr. Chairman, it is not a question of whether I am satisfied but of whether the people of Saskatchewan are satisfied. I ask the minister to consider improving facilities north of Lac La Ronge with a view to servicing commercially this particular area of the province.
I will conclude my remarks after two more questions to the minister respecting items relating to the province of Saskatchewan. Would the government give consideration to establishing an international airport within the province, something we do not presently have? All that is required is the provision of around-the-clock customs
Estimates
facilities, not a substantial undertaking. Since several airports are being renovated it seems to me now is an appropriate time to establish an international airport with around-the-clock customs facilities.
In conjunction with that would the minister consider making representations to Air Canada or to the CNR, as the case may be, to provide air freight service to Saskatoon? It seem to me that this kind of service should be provided to a province that is located in the heart of western Canada.

I am sure the hon. gentleman understands that international airports can only be established by agreement between two countries, such as the United States and Canada. Air lines must be prepared to fly to those airports. In my home town, Quebec city, which is the capital of Quebec, no international airlines want to serve the airport there. Even if an agreement were reached with the United States or with Europe that Quebec City should be on an international route, no air line would be interested in flying DC-8's or 747's to Quebec city. So there would be no point in extending the runway to enable 747's to land at Quebec city. The hon. member sees that I have a problem very similar to his.

Mr. Chairman, the city of Quebec is a great city, but in Saskatoon there are people who want to fly direct to the United States. This is why we would like the minister to establish an international airport in the province. Once he gets over the first hurdle of reaching an agreement, the second hurdle will be cleared very easily.

I have a few questions for the minister which I think he can answer quite briefly, and perhaps I will have one or two comments to make after he is finished. The first question is essentially the same one I asked today during the question period, to which I did not get an answer. It relates to a letter sent out on October 9, 1974, by Diane Waller, the minister's research assistant. It states in part:
Last year, the CTC's research branch carried out a thorough study of transportation services in the area and came to the conclusion that rail passenger services were not supportable by the population and that the preferred method of travel would be an improved rationalized bus service, a possible link to the existing main line passenger trains between London and Toronto.
The letter continues that "one primary candidate area" for replacement of the railway passenger service with bus services would be southwestern Ontario and it states that such action would be "in the national interest" and "should be encouraged and financially supported by the federal government".
My question is: did the minister authorize that letter to be sent?
I think the hon. gentleman told me he did not get an answer this afternoon. I think I gave him an answer.
What was the answer?

I am supposed to meet with Mr. Rose.

October 23, 1974
Estimates

Oh, for heavens sake! You have to be kidding. That was not the question I asked the minister. I asked him whether he authorized that letter to be sent by Mrs. Waller. Was it sent out under his authority?
Would you be kind enough to table the document?
I would be delighted to table the letter.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.
Do you think he is making it up?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. There is no requirement for the hon. member to table the document.
Mr. Chairman, I have received a request and I would be glad to accede to it if I have unanimous consent to table the letter.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would remind hon. members that to do so would be entirely out of order. If we were to allow hon. members to table documents every day we would have a tremendous problem just picking them up. In any event this is not in order.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might have an answer to my question. Did the minister authorize that letter to be sent? Surely the minister does not have to ask his deputy minister whether he authorized the letter.
Let's hear the answer.
Sit down and let him answer.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to support the request for an answer. This is the point I was making this afternoon. It is obvious from the way the government behaves that its ministers are not responsible. They do not respond to questions asked in the House. The government House leader said here tonight that we could ask questions and it is for the minister to decide which he will answer. I want to know whether we are to get answers, or whether this is a joke.
Oh, oh!
Those fellows in the back can make as much noise as they like, but we want to know whether the minister is going to answer.

On that point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would not mind this coming from anybody else but the Leader of the Opposition, because he surely knows from his vast experience what it is to run a department with about 100,000 persons involved. To ask me on the floor of the House whether I sent a letter and what was the reply is not fair.
If the minister wants to say that he would like to check this out, I am sure the hon. member will accept that.
Hear, hear!
There are a lot of smart alecks behind the minister. We want to know the answer, and we are very serious about this.

You are right. If the Leader of the Opposition asks me to check if I did send the letter I will check that, or find out if I sent it or somebody else sent it under my name, or under someone else's name. I am ready to do the research and give an answer to the House.
When are you going to do it?

Mr. Chairman, I am wondering if perhaps the page could take a copy of the letter across to the minister in order that he might see if he sent it? After I asked the question this afternoon did the minister not bother to consult with his staff to get an answer?
What were you doing between six and eight?
Will you answer that?
That is not what you asked me to do this afternoon.
I asked for an answer, and if the minister was serious enough I am sure he would have checked.
Would you allow me, Sir, to give you an answer tomorrow or the day after?
Certainly, if you assure me I will get the answer.
Then let us not continue to take up the time of the House.
Why did the minister not answer in that way before, rather than evading it?
Why don't you learn a little sense?
My next question relates to the third part of the study by the Canadian Transport Commission in respect of southwestern Ontario passenger service. Has the minister released report number three?
Do you have it now?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You have had it since February.
Is it the intention of the minister to answer, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The minister has the opportunity to answer and it is up to him to decide whether he will reply.

This is the whole point. The minister has been asked a perfectly simple question, whether he has released the report. If he does not know the answer and would undertake to get the information I am sure that is perfectly satisfactory. Surely if the minister is not going to answer perfectly straightforward questions, that is

I!

October 23, 1974

another matter. We want to know whether this is a serious procedure or a farce.
I think the Leader of the Official Opposition is right. I should look up the information and give him an answer.
Why don't you do so?
Has the minister yet sent the report to the affected members of parliament, the provincial members and the municipal councils?
I don't know.
Will the minister answer the question, or does he need more time to check it?
Yes, certainly before 10.30.
He said "yes".

Mr. Chairman, several times the minister and his officials have made reference to a tri-level conference which was to be held in Ontario to discuss the problems of passenger transportation, including the first report of the CTC suggesting that "The three reports are to provide a basis for discussions at a tri-level governmental conference to be held early in 1974, at which, it is hoped, a definition of policy with regard to public transportation in midwestern Ontario-Bruce will be achieved. "When is that meeting scheduled for, Mr. Chairman?
Excuse me, sir. I am at fault as I did not listen to the question. Will you repeat it?
The question I asked was when is the tri-level conference, at which this report is supposed to be discussed, scheduled?

The tri-level conference is not organized by the Department of Transport but by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. If you want to ask the Minister of State for Urban Affairs when the tri-level conference is to be organized I am sure he will provide you with that information.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps if I pose my questions to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs he would give me better answers than those I get from the Minister of Transport.
Order, order.

Apparently the minister who is responsible for transportation policy does not have the foggiest idea as to when these discussions are to take place. I would ask the minister whether he has read report number three?
Mr. Chairman, I regret it but this is strictly a narrow; political attitude.
Oh, oh, oh, oh!

Order.
Estimates
You are being railroaded, Jean.

With that kind of a smile you will never win an election. The problem is that in the field of transportation the federal government is involved, the provincial government is involved, and the municipalities are involved. So if it is desired to have what we call a tri-partite meeting this must be organized by the Department of Urban Affairs.
That is not what I asked. Have you read the report?
No, I have not. Have you?
Mr. Chairman, is the minister telling us that he has had this report since it was prepared in February, 1974, and delivered to him, and since that time he has not yet read the report?
I did receive the report.
Did you read it?
That is none of your business.
Mr. Chairman, the minister is making a mockery of the proceedings of this House. He already indicated he has not read the report. He has had it since February, 1974, and has sat on it since then.

Mr. Chairman, it would be childish in this House to mention all the reports I read and those I do not read. If you have some time to spare, come to my office at eight o'clock in the morning and I will give you material to read for hours and hours.

What the minister is saying now is that he does not know whether he has read the report, or perhaps he does not care. That certainly is typical of his attitude. I am wondering whether he has discussed the report with his own officials, and whether he is satisfied with the methodology used in the survey?
The report is being discussed with officials of the Ontario government at all levels. It is to be discussed by Mr. Rose and myself.

That is not the question. I asked the minister whether he is satisfied with the methodology of the report. Does he feel it was fairly and competently prepared, and that the conclusions it draws are justified?
I know the hon. gentleman knows all these answers. I do not have all the answers, I regret to say.
Does the minister have any of them?
Mr. Rose does not have all those answers either.

I would hope he would have some answers which would be better than what the minister has been giving us so far. This survey, which was taken of more

October 23, 1974
Estimates
than 1,200 families in the area, was released to the minister in February, 1974, and he has yet to release the report to the public.
The study was supposed to have been used as a basis for tri-level discussions. The minister has yet to make the report available to the federal members of parliament from the area, or to the provincial members of parliament from the area, or to the municipal councils in the area. He has not yet read the report.
Maybe the hon. gentleman would tell us whose report it is.
Mr. Chairman, it was prepared by the Canadian Transport Commission. If the minister cannot get his hands on it I could lend him my copy.
Do you think I control the Canadian Transport Commission?

The report at page nine states:
In a letter sent April 3, 1973, to the Hon. E. J. Benson, President of the Canadian Transport Commission, the minister referred to expressions of concern by the public and members of parliament that public transport services in the region were inadequate or in some cases non-existent, and requested that the commission, in cooperation with provincial authorities, undertake a review of the situation.
Is it not established procedure that when a minister personally requests that a report be made the report is made available to him?

May I shed some light here. I am told by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs that on Friday he will meet with Mr. Rhodes Irving on this report and start the study in order to find a solution. Perhaps some day the Minister of Transport will be invited, but for the time being I am out of the picture.
The minister has been out of the picture for the whole of the two years that I have been here.
Oh, oh!

It is worth knowing about this report. It was prepared at the request of the minister for him. The minister has either refused or been incapable of answering any of the questions I have asked him. I want to make some general comments briefly with respect to this report. The report is a fallacious document. It was designed in such a way that it discriminates against railway passenger service in the area and is in favour of bus passenger service. It is a piece of flim flam.
The report was incompetently prepared. It asks such questions of respondents as whether they would rate comparatively the convenience of arrival and departure times of business and trains. Considering that there have not been any trains in the area for four years, it is hardly relevant for them to be asked for a judgment on departure and arrival times. It also asks for comparative judgments with respect to keeping door to door travel time to a minimum.
It is interesting to note that the report itself shows that fully half of the people in the region who were consulted live within five miles of a bus service, but that three quarters of them are 25 miles or more from train service.

How are they to respond to such a question, and how are they to respond to a question about keeping costs to a minimum for travel from door to door if it requires a person to take a cab for a 50 mile ride when a bus is available within five miles?
It has been the experience of people in southwestern Ontario that the government has systematically ignored their needs. The government has had this report, which was obviously designed to damage the case for the restoration of railway facilities. It sat on it throughout the election, although the minister had it delivered to him. During that time Liberal candidates were permitted to say that they were in favour of train service restoration, when in fact the government's recommendation here was obviously that buses should be preferred to trains. I ask the minister whether or not he is prepared to release the report? Will he table the report this week?
Is there a by-election in your riding next week? Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows very well that I am not at all bound by this report which was prepared by the CTC.
I ask the minister whether he will table the report in the House this week.
You have it already.

Yes or no? Other affected members of parliament from the area, including the hon. member for Bruce who is in the minister's own caucus, do not have copies of the report. Will he table it this week?
Apparently the minister is not willing to answer that question either. When the report is available I want to make an offer to members on the government side that, if the minister will not give them a copy of it, I would be willing to lend them mine. I hope that at the time they consider the report they will recognize the fact that the survey was incompetently carried out, and that it was structured in such a way as to destroy the case for the restoration of the railway service. I think it is incumbent upon anybody who goes to a tri-level conference, or to any other discussion dealing with the matter of the restoration of the railway passenger service in southwestern Ontario, to ensure it is fully understood that conclusions reached in Part III of the study are not valuable for any discussions and should be completely disregarded.
Mr. Chairman, I have only one word to add. I am very worried about the passenger train service in Canada, and particularly in southwestern Ontario.
So am I.
Maybe you do not believe it-and I do not mind that-but I do mind and I hope in a few years we are going to improve all this. We started with the Richmond Hill-Toronto-
That is not in our area.

Oh, that is past, but there are some future-
October 23, 1974
That is not in our area. That is Toronto.
Oh, yes; Toronto is not in Canada.
It is not in southwestern Ontario.

This part you are interested in, I am interested in too and I hope we are going to find a good passenger service. I believe deeply in this, and I hope that together we are going to do something that will be worth while for the people.
You are getting emotional.
No, I am not getting emotional and whatever CN and CP tell you, I will try to give this service to the people. If I do not succeed maybe somebody else will be found in Canada to do it.

Mr. Chairman, last March when he met representatives of the Canadian Railway Labour Association the minister is quoted as saying to them:
It the transportation situation continues in the mess it is now, I don't want to stay in this job. Someone else can manage this department.
Then he said:
I can't manage transportation in Canada. If you ask who is managing transportation policy, I say to you I don't know.
I am sorry to say it, Mr. Chairman, but on the basis of what we see tonight I think there is still nobody managing transportation policy.
That was last March, Mr. Chairman. A few months later we got into an election. The Prime Minister went across the country and talked about what the government would do to improve urban transportation if re-elected. He said that a government which he led would spend some $300 million for urban transportation in the next five years, that it would pay out $100 million for transit vehicles, and $50 million for commuter vehicles. Mr. Chairman, that is a small percentage of what we are likely to require.
The Prime Minister promised that the federal government would pay 25 per cent of the cost of urban transit vehicles-buses, street cars, subway cars. Toronto alone estimates it will need 200 new subway cars and 200 new street cars in the next five years. Montreal expects to need 400 new subway cars in the next five years, and will be spending something over $400 million on the electrified subway system to link Dorval and the Mirabelle airport. Other cities also need buses and subway trains. A rough estimate is that in the next five years they will be spending over $900 million for urban transit, which is twice as much as the Prime Minister promised during the election.
I should like to ask the minister whether his department is reviewing the needs of the cities in the field of urban transit, whether it will increase the $100 million which the Prime Minister promised and, if not, when the cities can begin to see some of that $100 million which he promised during the election?
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt we intend to review that.

Mr.Chairman, at one point during this sad evening the minister asked us not to be political or parti-
Estimates
san. I am simply asking when the people in the cities of Canada, who elected a large number of Liberal members, will begin to see some of this $100 million which the Prime Minister promised during the election campaign?
The Prime Minister also promised $50 million over the next 10 years for commuter vehicles, mainly trains. Commuter vehicles in Canada are essentially used to bring people into Toronto and Montreal. I know the minister is very interested in Montreal. Can the minister tell us when the cities can expect some assistance with the purchase of buses and subway cars? When will the people of Toronto, Montreal, and their suburbs see some of the money for commuter cars which the Prime Minister talked about during the election?

Mr. Chairman, there are a certain number of things I cannot stand. One is this narrow way of tackling problems by saying, "You are interested in Montreal". My constituency is in Quebec, not Montreal. I am interested in Vancouver, Calgary, Winnipeg, Hamilton, Halifax and all the rest of Canada. That is why I am in this House. No one can find anything that I have done since I have been here-
Hear, hear!

I presume the applause will extend to the next part of my statement. I have not done anything for political purposes. I am in politics and like all members I believe in this country. As a minister, I believe I should serve all the country, not just part.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, this is the first time this evening I have found anything to agree with which the minister has said. He says that he is not a minister who represents only the city of Quebec. I am not a member who represents only the city of Winnipeg.
I do not think there is anything wrong with asking the minister when we can expect some action on a promise which his leader, the Prime Minister, made during the election, namely, that the federal government is prepared to spend $100 million for buses and subway cars and $50 million for commuter trains. Because I am not from Toronto or Montreal I do not think it is improper for me to ask the minister if the Prime Minister was serious when he made those promises? If he was serious, when will we begin to see the implementation of those promises? I have not received an answer to those two questions.
A few minutes ago the minister said there is one thing he is interested in, and that is improving passenger service. Even if the CNR and CPR are not interested, by God he will see that they improve passenger services or there will have to be another minister.
Let me go to another promise which was made. The Prime Minister promised that the government would set up an inter-city passenger rail service. A new Crown agency, the Canadian passenger transportation corporation, would be established to take over all inter-city passenger rail service.

October 23, 1974
Estimates
Three steps would be needed to implement such a policy. Legislation would be required to set up a corporation. We would need to introduce high speed inter-city trains, and introduce new concepts of rail travel leading to the elimination of level crossings and so on. This would take between seven and ten years to achieve. I am wondering when we are to see the beginning of this Canadian passenger transport corporation.
I used to find it most convenient to take one of the many trains between Ottawa and Montreal. Nowadays there are not many trains on this service. Meanwhile, the government is investing hundreds of millions in developing the STOL aircraft. Will the minister continue putting more millions into STOL, which will only meet the needs of a few highflying executives, or will he go back and give us some really good rail service between Ottawa and Montreal?

Mr. Chairman, I would be tempted to be mean and I believe I shall not resist the temptation. It is rather strange that that hon. member, who is well known in Canada, whom I met before going into politics, who even came to see me at the time when I was general secretary of the Confederation of National Trade Unions fighting for the rights of man, then seemed to be very objective.
Today, of the two figures quoted for the STOL experiment, that is mine of $25 million and that of Mr. Sinclair, chairman of the CP, he chooses the latter's, naturally. Of course, I recognize the great socialist spirit of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow): In any event, I say simply-it may be mean but not quite as much as the hon. member has been-that on March 7 last, I made a speech in the House on the transportation system, and then a general election was called much sooner than I had foreseen.
Mr. Chairman, during the election campaign, we said exactly the same things that we had said in our speech. In the Speech from the Throne, we find again exactly the same promises. We are about to come up with the programs we announced then. Let anyone find a government, whether NDP, Liberal or Progressive Conservative, which was as quick as this one has been and I shall raise my hat to him. If he cannot find one, I will just say that this is the meanness of a man who is unworthy of the great ideas he is fighting for.

Even on one of his bad days-and this is one of his bad days-when the minister gets angry he is a good stump speaker. I have been around this place and other legislative bodies long enough to know that any government, particularly a Liberal government, takes a long time before it implements new programs.
If the minister believes it is going to take some time to set up the Canadian passenger transport corporation I would not argue with him. But the Prime Minister, when he made that promise, gave some specific figures-$100 million for transit vehicles, $50 million for commuter vehicles, $50 million for research and development, $25 million

for rail relocation and $75 million resulting from the removal of the 12 per cent sales tax. This represents a package of $300 million over five years. I want to know whether the Prime Minister meant that this $300 million would be spent three years from now, in other words, just before the next election.
A sum of $300 million over five years means $60 million a year. I am not saying that we have to spend $60 million each year, but will any of this money be spent in the next year? That is a very simple question I should like to have answered. I am trying to be as objective as I can, and to get some idea what the Prime Minister meant when he made these promises to the people of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the less time we waste in the House because of the hon. member, the quicker we shall come to the projects mentioned in the Speech from the Throne.

Someone says I should raise a question of privilege, but I do not need to do so. If the minister really believes that asking questions in the House, or outside the House, about when the people of Canada can expect to get a program promised them by the Prime Minister is wasting the time of the House, then I might as well sit down now, Mr. Chairman.
There was not much point sitting on a Wednesday evening.

Mr. Chairman, my question is extremely brief and there may be time for one or two more before we break at 10.30. Unlike some of the questions asking for information asked a few minutes ago, the minister has had lots of time to consider my question. I have asked him this in correspondence over a number of months. I asked him last week in the House, and he promised me that he would have the answer. Now a week later I once again ask him whether we are going to get the report on the fatal accident at Frobisher Bay involving an aircraft and, if so, when?

Mr. Chairman, all I can say is that the report is on my desk. I informed some members of the House that I had the report; it has not been translated yet, and that is all. If the House would give unanimous consent to accepting the report without its being translated, then I am ready to table it, but I doubt whether that is a good procedure. I have the report, and I have told important people in the House that I have it.
If I may continue, would the minister, who promised me the report would be tabled last week, tell me when the report in both languages will be tabled?
If the hon. gentleman can tell me how long it takes to translate the report, I will give him the exact hour when it will be tabled.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has been good enough to send me over a note saying that he had a copy of the report. I do not think it would be any abuse of confidentiality to tell the committee that the minister
October 23, 1974

would either let me see it, or he would table it with consent. I sent him back a note saying that in the circumstances it would be advisable for him to table the report without waiting for the translation.

I think the Leader of the Opposition is entirely right. He told me that as leader of his party he did not oppose the tabling of the report in the circumstances outlined. Unfortunately, I have not had the same response from the other leaders.

Mr. Chairman, before we see the clock at 10.30, the minister suggested earlier in the evening that he was prepared to introduce a bill in the House very soon requiring disclosure from CPR and CNR of all relevant information in terms of determining real cost. Can we get

from the minister tonight some clear indication of precisely when he expects to do this?
I am in the hands of the House leader on this. As soon as he tells me that he has the agreement of all parties-
He has it now.

I think it would be a good thing to have it as fast as we can.
Progress reported.
